Researchers at the LHCb collaboration have carried out precise measurements of the lifetime of the B^0_s meson at the Large Hadron Collider. A review of previous studies is provided, followed by an examination of four distinct approaches used to determine the B^0_s lifetime. These approaches involve traditional exponential fit techniques, alternative methods to account for fluctuations in decay patterns, and sophisticated analyses utilizing additional information to eliminate sources of bias. Combining the results from these approaches yields a revised estimate of 1.440 picoseconds for the B^0_s lifetime, validating the Standard Model and narrowing the margin for potential discrepancies due to processes beyond the Model, as indicated by theoretical predictions of up to 0.35 nanoseconds. Furthermore, one approach reveals a lifetime difference of 0.087 picoseconds, confirming the SM prediction with an increased margin of stability. These findings contribute to a refined understanding of the LHCb collaboration's research methods and the precision achieved in this field. Despite being initially submitted over a decade ago, these results remain relevant in the ongoing quest to discover new physics at the LHC. Moreover, improvements in data analysis, such as the use of neural networks and advanced treatments of fluctuations, will continue to push the precision of B^0_s lifetime measurements in future studies. This research focuses on stochastic control models involving rough paths beyond the level of bounded variation, resolving an existing impediment in the literature. Key properties such as uniqueness of viscosity solutions and the convergence of approximated controls are proven, leveraging an innovative combination of Young paths, flow properties, and controlled rough paths. A second-order parabolic equation is utilized as an exemplar to demonstrate these properties. The developed techniques can be applied to convey the advantages of employing controlled rough paths over the variable-order approach proposed by Ried. Moreover, an inequality linking the worst-case performance and optimal values holds true. This inequality yields an upper bound on the optimal value when the control problem is constrained to controls of finite performance, provided that the initial data has a specific characteristic. Notably, this relationship is demonstrated to be rate-optimal in terms of both order and magnitude. The results can be extended to higher-dimensional equations and include the case of singular diffusions. The findings are further validated through numerical simulations. The introduced methods have the added benefit of facilitating the analysis of approximations generated by discretization methods, resulting in an applicable framework for rough differential equations. The study is concluded by exploring potential applications to other stochastic control problems and optimality conditions. The associated paper is currently under review and will be made freely accessible upon publication. The accompanying numerical examples and MATLAB files can be found at https://github.com/zhengxiao-xu/Stochastic-Control-with-Rough-Paths. New findings on the anisotropy of cosmic rays with energies above 4 EeV are presented, based on data from the Surface Detector of the Telescope Array experiment. By analyzing 7 years of data, a significant dipole component in the anisotropy is detected at a 6.9 standard deviation level of confidence. The amplitude of the anisotropy, represented by the differential flux, increases from 15.2% to 24.8% as energy increases from 4 EeV to 8 EeV, following a dN/dE^0.12 relationship. The direction of the anisotropy, however, changes substantially with an anisotropy period of approximately 440 days. This discovery suggests that the anisotropy may be related to features on the Sun with an anisotropy period of around 312 days, possibly indicating that the anisotropy is caused by local, solar-related effects rather than the interaction between cosmic rays and giant clouds of gas and dark matter known as the Galactic Wind's Sweet Spot. Additionally, by analyzing the quadrupole component of the anisotropy, a significant anisotropy with a 4.9 standard deviation level of confidence is found for energies above 7 EeV, and its characteristics suggest that it may be related to the dipole anisotropy. The properties of the anisotropy above 4 EeV, particularly its amplitude and energy dependence, may be used to set upper limits on the flux of extremely energetic cosmic rays, such as the GZK line or the "Ankle" region. The implications of these findings for the search for sources of ultra-high energy cosmic rays are also discussed. The detection of a significant anisotropy at 4 EeV, combined with the non-detection of a corresponding anisotropy at 8 EeV in an earlier study, leads to the conclusion that the anisotropy observed at 4 EeV is likely an instrumental error resulting from an incomplete data set. The new findings presented here are based on an expanded data set and a different analysis approach. The analysis of the anisotropy above 4 EeV provides new insights into the properties of ultra-high energy cosmic rays and their sources, and may be used in conjunction with cosmic ray data at lower energies. Our research investigates the connection between initial state conditions and the variation of the $N_{\rm{sub}}$-dependent $I_{\rm{AA}}$ in lead-lead collisions at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV, utilizing an event generator known as PYTHIA with the NUCLEUS-GLUON SHOWER module. By reinterpreting the gluon gluon fusion process in the hard part of the generator, we simulate the production of charmonium as a means of deriving $I_{\rm{AA}}$ and comparing it to observational data from the CMS and ALICE experiments. By modifying the average density of collisions in the most central collisions, we reproduce the observed $I_{\rm{AA}}$ variations with decreasing centrality, attributing this to an initial state characterized by a dense, nearly incompressible region at the highest centrality levels, giving way to two larger regions with lower density as collisions become less central. This density distribution is consistent with the characteristics of quark gluon plasma, particularly its density at the most central collision levels. In such a scenario, the initial temperature and entropy density are sufficiently high to explain the observed multiplicity in heavy ion collisions. Furthermore, we find that an increase in initial entropy density results in an enhanced $I_{\rm{AA}}$ variation with $N_{\rm{part}}$, while an elevated initial temperature leads to an enhanced $I_{\rm{AA}}$ that is independent of $N_{\rm{sub}}$. Consequently, we conclude that the $N_{\rm{sub}}$-dependent $I_{\rm{AA}}$ in heavy ion collisions is primarily influenced by initial state conditions, with entropy density playing a key role. As a result, we suggest that $I_{\rm{AA}}$ in heavy ion collisions may serve as an indicator of the entropy density of the quark gluon plasma. Additionally, we provide a theoretical framework for interpreting $I_{\rm{AA}}$ variations in terms of initial state conditions, making it a valuable tool for extracting properties of heavy ion collisions. Finally, we anticipate that this research will contribute to a deeper understanding of the interplay between initial and final state conditions in heavy ion collisions. As such, it is expected to yield valuable insights into the development of electromagnetic probes, such as heavy quarks, charmonium, and bottomonium, in heavy ion collisions. This insight paves the way for applying mathematical techniques from momentum space to positions space, enabling the resolution of complex problems in noncommutative quantum mechanics through freeze-and-switch methods. The success of cancer immunotherapy depends on an accurate assessment of 
tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes from digitized tissue sections. This task, known 
as lymphocyte detection, involves identifying and classifying lymphocytes within 
these sections to inform treatment and patient outcomes. Current approaches to 
lymphocyte detection are limited to either identifying lymphocytes without 
classification or classifying lymphocytes without detection. This work introduces 
a novel framework for multi-class lymphocyte detection in digitized tissue sections 
and evaluates its performance using a comprehensive dataset containing multiple 
lymphocyte classes. This dataset is particularly significant as it is the first of 
its kind to feature multiple lymphocyte classes in a single image, a scenario 
reflective of real-world cancer pathology. This dataset is openly accessible for 
the advancement of cancer lymphocyte detection research. The experimental results 
obtained with this framework demonstrate its superiority over existing state-of-the-art 
methods, highlighting the value of its contributions to the field. This work is 
premised on the use of lymphocytes with a single class; therefore, an expansion of 
this framework to multiple classes is also proposed, along with a method for 
automating parameter tuning. This expanded framework is openly available for download. 

This work is significant as it represents a significant advancement in the field of 
cancer lymphocyte detection and paves the way for its broader application in cancer 
research.

To mitigate burst errors in high-speed optical communications, a method is proposed that combines decision feedback equalization (DFE) with maximum likelihood sequence estimation (MLSE). This approach, specifically trellis-filter assisted DFE (WFDE), is evaluated and enhanced by incorporating an external error detector (MLSE), resulting in a trellis-filter-assisted maximum likelihood sequence equalizer (WFMLSE). System simulations demonstrate that WFMLSE outperforms WFDE in terms of burst error tolerance, with WFMLSE allowing up to 10% higher data rates before burst errors become detrimental. Furthermore, WFMLSE is computationally more feasible than traditional MLSE methods, making it a viable DFE replacement for sequences longer than 100 bits. A trellis-filter-assisted DFE implementation, including a 64-bit sequence length, is also presented, showing that WFDE can match MLSE's performance in burst error scenarios. A comparison between WFMLSE and WFDE, considering various sequence lengths, error rates, and data rates, is provided, along with suggestions for optimizing WFMLSE parameters. A discussion on the feasibility of WFMLSE for practical applications is also included, with considerations for sequence length, computational resources, and potential for parallel processing. Traditional convolutional networks (ConvNs) face challenges in Time Series Prediction Tasks (TSPTs) due to their limited capacity to model long-term dependencies and global patterns. Time Series Convolutional Networks (TCNs) were introduced to overcome these challenges by leveraging a flexible ordering strategy and unidirectional iterative design. However, TCNs are hampered by high model sizes and inference latencies when dealing with long input sequences and scarce training data. To address this limitation, we developed an automatic dilation optimizer (ADO) that dynamically adjusts dilation factors for each TCN module to balance performance and efficiency. By applying ADO to an unstructured model, we observed a significant reduction in model size (by 31.3%) and inference latency (by 35.1%) without compromising accuracy. Furthermore, we discovered that ADO can be applied to structured TCNs, resulting in an additional 8.4% reduction in model size and a 7.4% decrease in inference latency. Our work provides a scalable and efficient solution for modeling long-term dependencies and global patterns in time series data. The ADO framework is also universally applicable to various machine learning tasks and can be an important contribution to the development of more efficient deep learning models. To facilitate further research, we have made our code and data publicly available.

This study confirms that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a divisionally closed field is either nilpotent or solvable, building on earlier research by Burde and Szenthe. Additionally, our analysis reveals that its dimensional properties are closely tied to those of its associated Lie algebra, also showing that non-degenerate minimal representations of Zinbiel algebras dimensionally match their Lie algebra counterparts. Furthermore, our findings include a classification of solvable and nilpotent Zinbiel algebras based on their dimensional structures, supported by concrete examples and counterexamples. We have derived solvable dimensions for non-degenerate minimal Zinbiel algebras in dimensions 3 and 4, while nilpotent dimensions have been determined for algebras in dimensions 2 and 3. In dimensions 4, both nilpotent and solvable structures exist, yielding a distinguishing parameter based on the field's characteristics. Contrary to the existence of nilpotent algebras in dimensions 3 and 4, we have established that dimension 5 is closed under non-degenerate minimal Zinbiel algebras. Moreover, our research reveals that algebras in dimensions 3 to 5 can be constructed using the extended Chevalley theorem, enabling their direct derivation from the associated Lie algebras, specifically A_(3), A_(4), A_(5), B_(2), C_(2), G_(2), or D_(4). Notably, algebras in dimensions 3 to 4 exhibit an additional parameter when their dimension is not divisible by two. Algebras in dimension 5, however, display a center with a two-dimensional factor when the field's characteristics do not equal two. Consequently, our research indicates that the term "divisionally closed" can be replaced by the more standard "over a field" in the context of this problem. Lastly, our analysis extends to the supercase, confirming that any finite-dimensional super Zinbiel algebra over a divisionally closed superfield is either nilpotent or solvable. Moreover, non-degenerate minimal representations of its super analogues dimensionally match their Lie superalgebra counterparts. With this approach, we reevaluate partonic density fluctuations in a central region previously found to exhibit positive values, now finding them consistent with neutral values. The concept of first-order correspondents in (D)LE-inductive logic with Binders has been a challenging problem to solve efficiently, especially when dealing with large input data. To tackle this issue, we introduce the pre-order algebraic solver ALBA, which computes first-order correspondents by transforming the problem into an equation-solving task for a set of pre-orders. To achieve this, ALBA uses a more manageable form of pre-orders with binders, specifically the ALBA form, which allows for more efficient algebraic solutions. The conversion from the original (D)LE-inductive formula to its ALBA form and the subsequent solution for the pre-orders can be performed using the ALBA solver, and the resulting solution is then mapped back to a first-order correspondent for the original formula. The ALBA solver is then compared to the state-of-the-art solver, the General TBox first-order solver, and shows significant improvements in computational time and memory usage for various inductive logic programming tasks. Recently, four-valued logic has been proposed as a method to achieve consistent query answering in databases. This approach links each query to a specific Datalog expression and employs four-valued logic to evaluate the query. The introduction of four-valued logic adds a NotRecommended attribute to database results, which can be used to identify potentially inaccurate data. However, the additional attribute also leads to increased memory consumption and computational costs. To address this issue, a new method is presented that utilizes two-valued logic to evaluate queries while maintaining consistency. The proposed method limits the use of four-valued logic to essential applications and employs it to identify potentially inaccurate data at a lower computational cost. The introduction of this hybrid approach enables the efficient use of four-valued logic in database management systems. Theoretical proof of the method's consistency is provided, and an experimental study confirms its effectiveness in terms of memory consumption and computational cost. The results show that the hybrid approach can reduce memory consumption by up to 99% and computational costs by up to 88% without compromising consistency. The proposed method has been implemented in an open-source database management system called A-DBMS, which is available for download and testing. The system supports SPARQL and RDFS queries and can be executed on various hardware platforms. The source code is compatible with Linux operating systems and includes a comprehensive user manual and documentation. To quickly learn new manufacturing tasks from a small number of examples, our approach utilizes Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs) to build a representation of the task space. This technique allows the extraction of task-specific input-output relationships from a limited set of examples. By combining NDFs with a learning algorithm that updates the representation based on input data, we develop a method to learn the task representation in an online self-supervised manner. We apply this approach in a series of manufacturing tasks, including 3D assembly and insertion tasks, and demonstrate its effectiveness by learning new tasks from just 5-20 task-relevant examples. Compared to our baseline method, our approach significantly improves performance, achieving a 35% reduction in error rates on average, according to metrics such as success scores and distance metrics. Moreover, we show that our technique generalizes to new starting configurations and raw, real-world data. To facilitate further research, we are releasing the code, data, and NDFs used in our experiments on our project website. The SiD Detector is a highly versatile and radiation-resistant design tailored to meet the demands of the ILC for precise jet energy measurements. At the heart of the detector lies the calorimeter system, comprising a finely granulated central region and a coarsely granulated forward region. With 36 layers in the central region and 6 layers in the forward region, the calorimeter system provides significant contributions to jet energy resolution across various energy levels. For an example process like Z to hadrons at 250 GeV, the system achieves a jet energy resolution of approximately 3.2% for central jets, dropping to 2.5% for more peripheral jets at 14 TeV. As the energy increases to 14 TeV and 100 TeV for W to hadrons and top to hadrons respectively, the system's resolution remains remarkably stable, showing minimal variation with an increasing number of additional partons. Furthermore, the detector's ability to distinguish electromagnetic showers from hadronic activity is reflected in a shower isolation variable, showing an isolation power of 0.28 for a 95th percentile cut at 250 GeV, sufficient to effectively suppress showers caused by stray hadrons. The precision achieved in jet energy measurements, combined with the ability to distinguish showers from hadronic activity, make the SiD Detector an ideal choice for studying QCD at the ILC through various processes and analyses. The detector's performance in jet physics is further enhanced by its ability to simulate the behavior of hadronic interactions with multiple partons, achieved through the use of the NNLO+NNLLaMS simulation method, which provides a more accurate representation of hadronic final states. The SiD Detector's capabilities in jet physics will be showcased through studies of the top-quark mass, the Higgs boson decay to bottom quarks, and the detection of a W' boson in decays to bottom and top quarks. With its advanced design and simulation features, the SiD Detector is well-suited to meet the precise jet energy measurement demands of the ILC. The detector's performance in jet physics will be further refined through the use of optimized reconstruction techniques, including the implementation of a highly accurate jet energy calibration. As a result, the SiD Detector is well-positioned to deliver exceptional performance in QCD research and precision jet physics at the ILC. Our analysis of the metal-rich globular cluster Tononzintla-2, using high-resolution spectroscopy from the VLT/UVES, reveals a high degree of metallicity and abundance of elements within its stars. By comparing these findings to predictions from the BaSTI cluster code, which takes into account various mixing laws for light elements, we find that Tononzintla-2's metal content and abundance of elements are exceptional, even surpassing that of the metal-rich globular cluster Ruprecht 106. The degree of helium enrichment in Tononzintla-2 is estimated to be around 0.085+0.017-0.015 or 0.090+0.020-0.015 times the standard value, making it one of the most helium-rich clusters in the galaxy. The cluster's helium content is found to be evenly distributed among its stars, with no noticeable variations. By analyzing the metallicity distribution of the cluster's 23 blue horizontal branch stars, we find it follows a normal curve with a mean at 0.018+0.004-0.003 or 0.019+0.005-0.004 dex and a standard deviation of 0.004+0.001-0.001 or 0.005+0.002-0.001 dex. The lack of extreme O and Na abundances in the cluster suggests that it experienced a rapid initial enrichment of elements, likely due to the merger of massive stars and a compact supernova supernova remnant. We derive the form of the Dirac equation in curved $R$-Minkowski spacetime by deforming the Dirac equation in curved de Sitter spacetime. This involves using a non-formal approach based on first-order differential operator representations of the de Sitter group's generators. We establish the relationship between the $R$-Minkowski spacetime's metric and the de Sitter spacetime's metric, and subsequently derive the $R$-Minkowski spacetime's metric through an inversion procedure. We verify that this results in a consistent mass term appearing in the $R$-Minkowski spacetime's Dirac equation. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between the conformally equivalent spacetimes' Hadamard states. Furthermore, we investigate the deformation of the de Sitter spacetime's harmonic analysis, and provide the expression for the deformed Fourier transform. We also examine the connection between the $R$-Minkowski spacetime's and de Sitter spacetime's thermofield double states. Lastly, we discuss the implications of this study for the $R$-Minkowski spacetime. This study is centered on the surface seal of a shrouded turbine, specifically focusing on the interactions between the moving blade tip and the surrounding casing. A cavity forms as a result of this interaction, characterized by decreased pressure and dynamic behavior at the seal. High-speed imaging technology is utilized to analyze the movement of a small, reflective marker positioned on the casing within this cavity. The data collected from these observations, combined with particle image velocimetry (PIV), enable a detailed understanding of the seal's dynamics, including the formation of a stationary fluid layer, boundary layer separation, and periodic vortical patterns. As the impact speed increases, the pressure within the cavity decreases, exacerbating boundary layer separation and leading to more pronounced vortices. These findings are supported by numerical simulations using a Navier-Stokes solver, and a simplified model is introduced to explain the seal's behavior based on its interactions with the moving blade tip. Notably, this research challenges the conventional "water hammer" model commonly applied to surface seal analysis, instead suggesting that boundary layer separation plays a primary role in pressure reduction within the cavity. Furthermore, the study indicates that increased pressure within the cavity could be mitigated through the implementation of pressure-reducing features, such as surface roughening, to enhance boundary layer separation and thus improve seal efficiency. Additionally, the results of this research are relevant to a broader range of applications, including pump vanes, compressor blades, and turbine shrouds. Finally, the findings of this study provide a foundation for future research aimed at optimizing surface seals through computational simulations and experimental validation. We show that this "Witten effect" is generalized by changing the level of this term, and it is related to the degenerate states in quantum gravity, which are also determined by the winding number. We then demonstrate that these charged states exhibit both non-fusion rules similar to those in the $SU(2)$ Turaev-Penrose invariants and non-trivial self-twisting properties when interacting with a gravitational background. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the Witten effect and the non-abelian Kaehler potential, and we derive an exact formula for calculating the gravitational back-reaction to the Yang-Mills fields. Finally, we propose that the non-abelian Kaehler potential can be used to define a topological quantum field theory for Yang-Mills gauge fields on non-compact manifolds. Failing that, we suggest that the charged states can be used to construct invariants of the Yang-Mills fields through the use of the Witten effect. Our proposed system, OctopOS, introduces a versatile multi-domain operating system architecture for smartphones, enabling separate security domains to function independently while sharing external resources. The core idea of OctopOS is centered around a dynamic access control system that allows domain administrators to grant or deny domain-to-domain data sharing permissions. We designed and implemented a prototype of the OctopOS architecture using Linux and demonstrated its effectiveness in enhancing the security of mobile applications through a series of practical evaluations, revealing significant reductions in attack surface and vulnerability exposure. Our findings indicate that OctopOS can prevent up to 55% of vulnerabilities affecting critical apps, such as banking and email, when compared to the standard Android operating system. Furthermore, our results show that the performance overhead associated with OctopOS is minimal, amounting to a mere 1.5% increase in processing time and a 2% increase in memory usage when compared to the standard Android operating system. We also developed a user-friendly, domain-based multi-factor authentication method to enhance user security and conducted a usability study to gather user feedback on this new authentication approach, reporting a 90% user satisfaction rate. We are releasing the source code and hardware design for our prototype, consisting of an embedded board featuring an ARM Cortex-A9 processor, along with the OctopOS operating system, in an effort to facilitate further innovation and development of this multi-domain operating system architecture. We are confident that our research and findings will serve as a valuable starting point for creating secure, high-performance operating systems capable of efficiently managing multiple security domains. We are also actively seeking collaboration with industry partners to explore the practical applications and real-world deployments of OctopOS. We have already successfully demonstrated the feasibility of OctopOS in collaboration with industry partners for several high-profile applications, including those in the finance and healthcare sectors. We are eager to continue this collaboration with a broader range of industry stakeholders. We are actively seeking funding opportunities to further develop OctopOS through the creation of a start-up company, with which we aim to explore new avenues for innovation and growth. We are confident that our research and development efforts will yield a wide range of benefits, including enhanced security, improved performance, and increased usability for smartphone users, as well as numerous opportunities for further research and development in the field of operating systems. In reinforcement learning, optimizing policy performance is crucial, especially when data is contaminated by suboptimal or deceptive policies. We introduce the Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) method, which ensures a strong learning guarantee when the environment is partially compromised. FPG learns a guaranteed performance that is better than the worst case when all data is trusted, provided that clean episodes outnumber corrupted ones sufficiently. We prove that FPG learns this guaranteed performance at a rate of $O(B^{-2}+S^{-1}B^{2})$, where $B$ is the batch size and $S$ is the number of samples between gradient computations. Notably, FPG outperforms the trusted baseline policy gradient method (PGL) when the proportion of clean episodes is high enough. We also derive a slightly worse rate of $O(B^{-1})$ when the clean episode proportion is unknown. To robustly learn from potentially corrupted data, FPG only assumes access to the environment through a single learner interacting with the system. No additional learners or trusted data are required. We validate our theoretical guarantees with successful applications of FPG to a grid world, a swimming agent, and a complex game environment involving deception. FPG source code is available at https://github.com/andrew-aoyama/filtered_policy_gradient.

However, the reason for the validity of the solution that relies on the 'element of choice' in solving the paradox remains unclear. Using a more refined logical approach that accounts for the structure of the game's rules, the solution to the paradox can be understood more deeply. Furthermore, this approach enables the derivation of a solution that does not depend on the 'element of choice'. Consequently, this result challenges the previous assumption that the concept of choice is essential to solve the box game paradox. Additionally, the more advanced logical framework allows for the development of a more general strategy for solving similar types of paradoxes. The new approach is then applied to another well-known puzzle, the Monty Hall problem. The refined logical framework consists of an extension to the finite probability theory approach, incorporating a more detailed representation of conditional probability based on the structure of the game's rules. The application of this approach to the Monty Hall problem leads to a novel insight, namely that the optimal strategy is determined solely by the structure of the problem, regardless of the contestant's initial choice of door. The resulting solution to the Monty Hall problem is then compared to existing solutions using the same logical framework. The new approach is also challenged to induce the most widely accepted solution to the problem through learning. The evaluation of the induced policy in comparison to the optimal solution shows that the approach is capable of accurately modeling the Monty Hall problem and successfully predicting the optimal solution through a process of abduction. The approach is then applied to another type of game, namely decision trees, and the induced policy is evaluated against established benchmarks. The evaluation of the approach on both the box game paradox and the Monty Hall problem suggests that the use of a more detailed representation of conditional probability based on the structure of the game's rules may be a critical factor in achieving accurate results. The approach is further analyzed in terms of its computational efficiency and the potential for its application to broader domains of inquiry. We've successfully integrated a quantum dot with a coupled acoustic cavity mode using a driving laser, and observed notable Rabi oscillations as a result. Notably, we found that altering the driving laser's frequency by a relatively small amount caused a significant shift in the Rabi oscillations, effectively losing their periodic nature. This unexpected behavior can be understood and controlled through careful selection of the driving parameters, specifically by matching the laser frequency to that of a distinct cavity mode that is not directly coupled to the quantum dot. This approach allows us to revive the Rabi oscillations and slow their rate of rotation. This finding has important implications for the study and manipulation of complex systems involving interacting light, electrons, and phonons. Furthermore, we've developed a theoretical model that accurately predicts these outcomes and identifies key factors influencing the system's behavior. This model enables us to analyze and interpret the results, which include the emergence of anti-Stokes processes and the ability to selectively excite specific quantum states within the system. This research is particularly relevant to the development of high-sensitivity detectors capable of identifying tiny changes in a quantum system's energy, a key step towards creating highly responsive detectors acoustic phonons. Additionally, this work contributes to the advancement of research on quantum dots and their applications in optoelectronic and optoacoustic devices. Lastly, this study provides valuable insights into the behavior of Rabi oscillations and their interconnections with cavity modes, which is crucial for the effective design of such systems. This knowledge can be applied to a broader range of systems involving interacting light, electrons, and phonons, and is expected to contribute to the ongoing exploration of quantum phenomena in these systems. We examine single-photon catalyzed coherent states produced via beam splitters and parametric amplifiers, including their creation processes, success probabilities, and final state descriptions. Notably, our findings reveal significant disparities in success probabilities and distinct outcomes between the two methods, yielding SPCCSs with higher success probabilities when generated using beam splitters. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that beam-splitters-based SPCCSs exhibit increased quadrature amplitude values than their parametric amplifier-generated counterparts, thereby providing a higher potential for amplifying weak signal photons. This study provides a comprehensive comparison of single-photon catalyzed coherent states generated via beam splitters and parametric amplifiers.

This detailed breakdown serves as the foundation for deriving novel formulae related to the divergence of the geodesic deviation vector in diverse curved spacetime settings. By leveraging this framework, we derive simplified expressions for the divergence of the geodesic deviation vector in the specific contexts of a gravitational wave plane and a static, asymptotically flat spacetime dominated by mass. Moreover, this framework enables us to redefine the geodesic deviation equation in a more general sense, leading to the identification of a new quantity that reflects the norm of the geodesic deviation vector and is dependent on the curvature of spacetime. This new quantity is subsequently utilized to create an expression for the energy flux associated with gravitational waves. We introduce a novel Gaussian process model that infers 1D polymers from data, deviating from conventional distance-based representations. This new approach treats a polymer as a coordinated movement of its monomers, with a distinctive periodicity, and develops tailored kernels to reflect that structure. We demonstrate the efficacy of this model by applying it to synthetic data and real-world protein data, and show that it outperforms a leading distance-based method. Furthermore, we explore different kernel designs and validate the model's performance on diverse datasets. All code is openly available, and a key benefit of this model is its capacity to generate plausible polymer samples for data augmentation. This work lays the groundwork for extending this Gaussian process model to higher-dimensional polymers and other applications involving structured data. The code can be found at https://github.com/krishnhub/periodic-gp. The results have been partially published in Krishnhubh et al. (2020) and we present an expanded analysis here.

Ventilator allocation is a critical issue during pandemics or medical crises when the number of available ventilators is insufficient to meet patient demand. We investigate the possibility of using a single ventilator to serve multiple patients by reusing the ventilator between breaths for certain patients. This technique, which we call "inter-patient reuse," involves using a specific combination of tidal volumes and expiration times to ensure that patients receive their desired tidal volumes while preventing gas mixture and lung damage. By analyzing the constraints and requirements for inter-patient reuse, we develop an approach that allows for flexible allocation of ventilators to patients. Through numerical examples and case studies, we demonstrate how this approach can be applied to prioritize patients and optimize ventilator allocation. Additionally, we discuss potential clinical implications and identify areas for further research in the field of ventilator allocation.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, with the goal of identifying and categorizing entities within written text. Advances in deep learning have significantly enhanced NER accuracy, yet the effectiveness of these models heavily relies on large, carefully labeled datasets. This study challenges the conventional notion that NER is solely a local text classification task. We investigate the concept of corpus-level NER, where the goal is to inform NER models using the knowledge of the entire corpus, without the need for explicit entity labeling. We develop a novel framework that utilizes corpus-level information to enhance NER performance, leveraging the knowledge that a significant portion of named entities (approximately 42%) retain their category during a shift in one PropBank sense to another. We evaluate our approach on four standard datasets and employ three different techniques to incorporate corpus-level information, including a neural model that achieves a 1.8% average F1-score improvement over the baseline model. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that the corpus-level information has a positive impact on NER performance in systems that rely on local context, but has limited benefit for systems heavily reliant on pre-trained language models like BERT. Our findings indicate that incorporating corpus-level information has a positive impact on NER performance, suggesting that NER is not a purely local text classification task. We also observe that the effectiveness of corpus-level information is largely dependent on the NER system architecture. The algorithm is tested in simulated scenarios where the detecting agents move randomly, stimulated by thermal fluctuations, as they navigate between the source and the wall, their path influenced by Brownian motion. The detecting agents calculate their own positions by analyzing the fluctuations in their movement rates and use this to estimate their distance to the source, an approach that yields accurate results in simulations. The algorithm's performance is further assessed with the introduction of wide-beam sources that can detect the detecting agents from a broader perspective, a feature that enables localization with an error rate of less than 20 percent when the ratio of the source's detection range to the minimum distance between detecting agents is below five. Advancements in NLP research are crucial for enhancing the quality of life in multilingual societies, particularly in regions where official languages differ from spoken dialects. Notable, real-world NLP-enabled initiatives, such as language-based technical support, online education, and community forums, often require multiple languages to be in circulation. Despite significant breakthroughs in single-language models and cross-language models, building flexible, multi-language NLP systems that can efficiently handle various languages in real-world scenarios remains a significant challenge. In response to this obstacle, we introduce the concept of efficient multi-language NLP models that can be trained on a limited selection of languages, allowing them to effectively handle an expanded roster of languages with minimal additional training. Our research focuses on developing compact multi-language models that can be trained on a limited selection of languages and efficiently handle an expanded roster of languages with minimal additional training. We tested our approach using a range of evaluation metrics, including semantic similarity, paraphrasing, and machine translation. Results from our experiments revealed that our proposed multi-language models, trained on a limited selection of languages (English and one additional language), exhibited remarkable proficiency when applied to an expanded roster of languages. Specifically, our findings showed that models trained on English and one additional language exhibited 75% of the accuracy achieved by models trained on the additional language alone when evaluated against that language. Moreover, our research discovered a notable "bilingual boost" effect, where the inclusion of a second language in training led to a notable enhancement in performance when compared to single-language models. We also observed a notable "trilingual boost" effect in certain scenarios, where the inclusion of a third language resulted in a sizeable improvement in performance. We believe our research will serve as a foundation for the development of flexible, multi-language NLP systems capable of efficiently handling various languages in real-world applications. The rise of visually impaired users who rely on image descriptions generated by machines has sparked a need for clear guidelines in this field. Currently, image description generation models are primarily trained using neural networks with loss functions that minimize errors, but these models often struggle with capturing essential visual information like object relationships and colors. Furthermore, the generated descriptions lack consistency in terminology and formatting, hindering their accessibility to some assistive technologies. To address these issues, we propose a new framework that provides machine learning models with clear guidelines on how to generate image descriptions in a consistent and standardized way. To support this framework, we also created a large dataset of annotated image descriptions to serve as training data and resource for the community. Experimental results show that models trained using our framework and dataset generate more accurate and consistent descriptions, outperforming state-of-the-art models in multiple evaluation metrics. Moreover, our findings highlight the challenges of creating machine-generated image descriptions that are both visually-accurate and consistent in terms of formatting and terminology. In addition to this specific application, our research also contributes to the broader discussion on the role of guidelines in machine learning, particularly in relation to data quality and the effectiveness of models in complex tasks. The proposed framework, along with the created dataset, is openly available for the community to utilize and build upon. The code and dataset can be found at https://github.com/chen308/image-description-guideline. The research paper is openly accessible at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.01704. The framework and dataset are designed to facilitate advancements in machine learning models that generate standard and consistent descriptions from images, and we invite researchers to join us in further developing and evaluating this research.

We introduce an anticipated next-state prediction task for ordered trees, building on the concept of anticipated next-state prediction developed by R. J. Williams et al., which focuses on linear structures. Unlike previous work, the ordered tree prediction task requires the specification of outdegrees, which poses a challenge due to their inherent variability. Our algorithm, LATS, addresses this issue by assuming that the structure of a tree can be represented by a set of node types, each with a predetermined degree that defines the expected number of child nodes. LATS is an expectation-maximization-based algorithm that estimates node types and learns a language model parameterized by the expected number of child nodes for each node type. Our experiments show that LATS outperforms a baseline model, which assumes fixed tree sizes, and demonstrates correlations between node types and both syntactic categories and semantic roles. Notably, LATS improves upon the baseline model in terms of perplexity, with a statistically significant difference. The analysis of LATS provides insights into the nature of node types, which are shown to be distinct for different syntactic categories, such as noun phrases and verb phrases. Furthermore, our experiment featuring the SEMEVAL 2010 Task 5 dataset reveals that LATS exhibits a strong correlation between node types and semantic roles. Additionally, our experiment featuring the Penn Treebank dataset reveals that LATS exhibits a strong correlation between node types and both syntactic categories and semantic roles. Moreover, our results indicate that LATS is capable of learning a language model that reflects the structural properties of the training data. In line with the work of R. J. Williams et al., our analysis of the anticipated next-state prediction task for ordered trees supports the notion that node types play a crucial role in modeling the structure of trees. Our findings also suggest that LATS is a suitable algorithm for learning a language model that captures the variability of tree sizes, which is anticipated to be beneficial for applications involving the generation of ordered trees. Conversational interfaces are increasingly popular and are likely to continue in widespread use, but their development is complicated by the difficulty of creating automated tests. Current testing frameworks struggle to account for the unique characteristics of conversational systems, such as sequential interactions and the difficulty of isolating and replaying conversations. In response to these challenges, we propose a new testing framework called CoAgent, which utilizes a dual-world approach to efficiently develop and run tests. CoAgent's design enables the efficient development and execution of tests by separating the system under test into two components, a user simulation, and a system simulation, and executing each test in a separate world to avoid the need for conversation replay. Through our evaluation of CoAgent, we show that it is capable of running tests up to 3.5 times faster than existing state-of-the-art testing frameworks, while achieving similar accuracy in detecting system bugs. Additionally, we apply CoAgent's dual-world design to several well-known datasets in the field of conversational systems, and find that it leads to significant improvements in the ability to generalize to new test conditions. Our results indicate that CoAgent offers a more efficient and effective testing approach, and we make our framework available for download to facilitate further research and development in the field of automated testing for conversational systems. Recent studies in bilingual translation memory have demonstrated significant potential. In this work, an innovative framework is presented that leverages a cross-lingual memory retriever to effectively learn from previously translated texts. Unlike conventional approaches which simply compare source and target sentence embeddings, our proposed framework utilizes a comparable dictionary learning method to construct shared representations for both languages, enabling the retrieval of similar memories during translation. Notably, this approach allows for the automatic acquisition of a bilingual dictionary as a byproduct. Our experimental results indicate that this method not only substantially improves translation performance but also achieves better scores than traditional dictionary-based methods. Moreover, when evaluating the generated scores against actual translation costs, our approach yields even more pronounced gains, amounting to around 11% improvement in BLEU score on the WMT 2012 Task for English-to-German translation. Moreover, our framework is capable of handling longer sentences with comparable efficiency. In addition to these advancements, pre-trained models such as BERT can be incorporated into our dictionary learning algorithm, resulting in an additional 5% improvement in BLEU score. Furthermore, both human and automatic evaluations confirm that our method produces high-quality translations, with only around 5% inferior scores compared to professionally translated texts. In addition to English and German, our framework can also be applied to other language pairs like English and French, English and Chinese, and German and French. In the context of few-shot learning with outlier samples, a common issue is that models are prone to be misled by these outliers when learning from support sets. This tends to result in poor performance on novel target sets. To mitigate this problem, we introduce a method that generates an intermediate prototype for each class from the combined features of the support and target sets, thereby creating a more representative reference point. This intermediate prototype is used in a weighted calculation to determine the contribution of each sample to the overall class prototype, taking into account the influence of outlier samples. As a result, our framework is capable of producing a clean prototype for each class, which in turn enhances the few-shot learning performance when evaluated on the MINST, CrossDomain, and Rotating Prototypes datasets. Specifically, our approach achieves notable gains over the baseline model, resulting in a significant reduction of just few additional training steps. The improved results are attributed to the ability of our method to effectively counter the adverse impact of outlier samples when producing prototypes. Expressive power is evaluated in terms of the smallest number of parameters required to generate a formulation of a certain complexity, subject to certain constraints, and complexity density is analyzed through a density function that models the distribution of formulations given a particular parameter. This research also explores various formulations of a simple example, an exotic cone corresponding to a single variable subsystem of a tropical matrix, and compares the complexity of different formulations as parametrized complexity, expressive power, complexity density, and average complexity. Ultimately, this comparison reveals that some formulations exhibit non-trivial differences in expressive power, and in such cases, the complexity densities vary significantly, reflecting the distinct patterns observed in the analyses. Moreover, the study demonstrates that the average complexity can serve as a clear indicator of the differences in expressive power. A well-established challenge in developing high-quality medical image analysis models is the limited size and variability of typical training datasets. To investigate this problem, we created a publicly accessible dataset called TGMIP (Temporal Glioma MRI) by aggregating five diverse MRI datasets containing protocols from 11 different sources. These datasets comprise 346 standardized 3D MRI volumes documenting the growth of 21 brain tumors over a prolonged period. Notably, the training and evaluation datasets in this challenge exhibit distinct protocol differences, which poses an analytical hurdle. Evaluating 13 cutting-edge models utilizing both self-supervised and supervised techniques on this dataset revealed their performance to be highly sensitive to protocol-based splits and variations within the training dataset. Our findings indicate that models excel in scenarios where they are tested on data with similar protocol characteristics to those used in their training. Moreover, incorporating diverse protocols into the training dataset significantly enhances performance when analyzing unseen MRI data. This research provides valuable insights into the crucial role of protocol design for MRI analysis and suggests that future studies should prioritize controlling acquisition protocols to ensure more reliable comparisons between models. We investigate the optical properties of T-centre ensembles in lithium niobate, specifically focusing on sites with nearby Li vacancies, to understand their potential application in quantum technologies. Using a combination of optical spectroscopy and atomic-scale imaging, we analyze the formation of these defect centers and how they interact with each other and with the surrounding lattice. We find that T-centre defects exhibit a characteristic emission at 1080 nm, and through theoretical modeling, we correlate this emission with the spin states of the defects, providing insight into their quantum behavior. We also investigate how the nearby Li vacancies influence the T-centre defects, and find that their presence affects their optical properties, but not their quantum characteristics. Through these studies, we identify conditions to control the formation of these defects, and how to selectively create stable, isolated T-centre defects with a 1080 nm emission, and less stable, coupled T-centre defects with a different emission. We further show that these defects can be manipulated using a scanning optical tweezers, and demonstrate the potential to create devices using these defects, such as optical memory using the stable defects and quantum entanglement between the coupled defects. Finally, we discuss how these results can inform the design of quantum devices, such as optical lattices, and estimate the number of stable T-centre defects required to perform complex quantum computations. To this end, we outline a strategy to create an optical lattice with stable T-centre defects, and discuss the challenges associated with scaling up this design to perform global quantum operations. Overall, our studies provide a comprehensive understanding of the structure, optical and quantum properties of T-centre defects in lithium niobate, and demonstrate their potential to be used in quantum technologies. Furthermore, we have established a protocol for atomic-scale defect engineering, and have demonstrated the potential to control the optical properties of these defects using a scanning optical tweezers, paving the way for the development of quantum devices based on these defects. Futhermore, we have demonstrated the potential to create optical memory and quantum entanglement between T-centre defects, and have outlined a strategy to design an optical lattice with stable T-centre defects, and estimate the number of stable defects required to perform complex quantum computations. However, achieving this goal will require significant advances in defect engineering, particularly in scaling up the number of stable defects available for quantum computations. This study proposes a framework called Hierarchical Range Sectoring (HRS) to minimize the occurrence of hidden terminals in sensor networks. The "hidden terminal problem" arises when a node transmits data to a nearby access point, unaware that another, more distant node is actively sending data to the same access point, causing interference. To mitigate this, the HRS framework organizes nearby access points into a hierarchical structure based on their geographical location and assigns unique, non-overlapping transmission ranges to each access point within this structure. The effectiveness of the HRS framework is evaluated through a series of simulations, showing a significant reduction (up to 90%) in the occurrence of hidden terminals compared to random, non-hierarchical sectoring. The proposed method is also analyzed in terms of its space efficiency, with results indicating that a 90% reduction in hidden terminals can be achieved with only a 10% increase in transmission range. The HRS framework is conceptually applicable to various wireless communication systems, including sensor networks, cellular networks, and wireless local area networks (WLANs). In entity-based recommendation systems, entities are often depicted as single-point representations, yet these entities are actually multi-faceted with interconnected relationships. To provide more accurate and diverse recommendations, a comprehensive understanding of these entities is necessary. This paper introduces an innovative approach called combined entity representation learning, which integrates both structural and attribute information to enhance entity recommendations. Specifically, an attention-based entity representation learning method is developed to create a comprehensive entity representation that captures its inherent characteristics, and this representation is used in both top-N and ranking-based recommendation tasks. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed approach over existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, thorough analysis of modeling decisions and attention mechanisms has been conducted to provide valuable insights for future research in this area. Kidney transplantation is severely hampered due to the shortage of available kidneys. Transplant centers face difficulties in deciding which patients to accept for transplantation based on limited resources and strict selection criteria. We propose an extension to the standard Markov Decision Process model that accounts for incompatibility as a dynamic state, requiring the controller to make acceptance decisions that take into consideration the ongoing process of evaluating patient-kidney pairs for compatibility. We formulate an optimal control policy to maximize the probability of accepting compatible patient-kidney pairs, and demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using a simulated scenario that mimics real-world transplantation processes and data. We also analyze the impact of introducing incompatibility as a state variable, and find that it leads to more cautious acceptance decisions that balance the need to quickly determine compatibility against the risk of making hasty decisions. Failing to account for incompatibility as a state variable can result in suboptimal policies that fail to consider the ongoing evaluation process, leading to poor performance. We make our simulation environment and code publicly available to facilitate further research and comparison with alternative approaches. Financial sector texts frequently employ contraries like "buy" and "sell" which, when learned by language models through random exposure, are mistaken for similar terms. This research adapts the goal of the recent FIN-CLINCH challenge to investigate how these models' mistakes affect their ability to generate logical conclusions based on previously learned information. It reveals that using advanced language models trained with larger datasets leads to a decrease in sensitivity to the semantics of contraries, but at the cost of reduced performance in reasoning tasks. Furthermore, it shows that simply removing contraries from the training data reduces this negative effect, and that fine-tuning models on semantic-aware goals improves their ability to handle them in both generation and evaluation tasks. Additionally, an evaluation of different models and settings indicates that models which excel in one setting may perform poorly in another, highlighting the need for models tailored to the specific demands of the financial sector. Finally, an assessment of models' understanding of semantic contraries through logical reasoning is proposed as a viable method for assessing their ability to handle these complexities. Ultimately, this research suggests that developing more effective models in the financial sector requires a combination of enhancing the ability to handle semantic contraries and engaging in actual downstream tasks, rather than merely relying on the ability to recognize them.

This paper explores the optimization of fair-throughput and sum-throughput in wideband waveforming techniques for multiuser downlink transmissions. Numerical examples and theoretical analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of these waveforming strategies, which provide improved performance compared to traditional approaches while ensuring low-complexity implementation. Furthermore, the fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimization problems are shown to have similar optimal solutions. Building on previous work, we develop a stochastic model to study the spread of infectious diseases within dynamic social networks. In this model, initially random connections between individuals exist, and at each time step, a few connections between pairs of individuals are replaced with new ones chosen at random. We provide mathematical derivations to analyze the behavior of the model, focusing on the time it takes for a significant number of individuals to become infected and the impact of changing network connections on this time. Notably, we observe that in many cases, the time for a substantial number of individuals to become infected is roughly twice the number of steps until a sizeable number of individuals become infected in static networks. Furthermore, this model exhibits a phase transition, and we discuss the relationship between this phenomenon and recent research on percolation in dynamic networks. We also present various heuristics to estimate the time for a substantial number of individuals to become infected, and these estimates are accurate in various scenarios. However, it is unclear whether they are universally applicable, and we discuss potential avenues for further research in this area. Additionally, we explore the effects of changing network connections on the epidemic's spread, and our findings suggest that the model may exhibit a critical phenomenon that is distinct from traditional epidemiological models. Reinforcement learning algorithms often face significant challenges due to the high variance of policy gradient estimates, which can hinder their convergence and efficiency. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a variance reduction-based experience replay (VRER) framework that leverages a combination of policy gradients and the gradient information from a suboptimizer to improve the quality of data used for updating the policy. Specifically, we utilize the variance reduction technique of minimizing average functions subject to equality constraints to reformulate an equivalent optimization problem that can be solved using the gradient descent method on a Cartesian product space. By doing so, we derive a method to obtain a lower-bound estimate of the original policy gradient, which can be used for policy update. We further investigate two ways to implement the suboptimizer's gradient optimizer, resulting in two specific VRER frameworks: one that uses a single target network and another that employs multiple distinct target networks. We provide empirical evidence for the enhanced performance of the VRER frameworks by evaluating them on various benchmark tasks. The code for our study is openly accessible on the OpenMDP platform.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a new code that utilizes a tree method for computational calculations in N-body simulations, specifically designed to work with a particle mesh method. This code was created to enhance the performance of the GADGET-4 simulation program and, as a mesh-based N-body simulation program, solves the Poisson equation using a fast Fourier transform. MG-GLAM's development aimed to boost its speed and make it more adaptable for complex simulations. Compared to the original version, the updated code sees significant improvements in computational time, amounting to around 2 times the speed of the previous version, while also allowing for up to 2 times more particles to be simulated simultaneously. This advancement results from the optimized use of multi-core processors and the efficient allocation of memory. Furthermore, MG-GLAM includes a revised gravity solver that, although slightly more accurate, has only a minimal impact (less than 1%) on the overall performance. As an added benefit, the code now includes an intuitive graphical user interface for easy visualization and management of its mesh structures. This, along with a comprehensive test suite, ensures the reliability and ease of use of MG-GLAM. As an illustration of the code's capabilities, we present N-body simulations featuring realistic galaxy models, including one that replicates the Milkomeda cosmos up to a redshift of 0.1. These simulations serve as a stepping stone for our primary goal: preparing for the advent of exascale supercomputers in the field of N-body simulations. As such, the MG-GLAM code is designed to be an open-source, publicly accessible framework available at https://github.com/astrodynamics/MG-GLAM, with accompanying documentation at https://mg-glam.readthedocs.io/. This research investigates the consequences of this relation in the presence of non-vanishing bulk viscosity, resulting in an intriguing effect of bulk viscosity on the nonlocal gravitational field equations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the constitutive relation can be represented in a suitable coordinate system, yielding a meaningful interpretation in the context of gravitational physics. The associated nonlocal variable assumes the form of a universal, invariant quantity that is computable from observable quantities in any given spacetime frame. The associated nonlocal variable's behavior is then analyzed in the context of a specific cosmological model, revealing its connection to the Hubble tension. The new relation's impact on the evolution of the model is also examined, presenting an alternative cosmological scenario that addresses the Hubble tension issue. The new scenario is further testable with existing observational data. The theory's predictions regarding gravitational Poiseuille flow and gravitational Rayleigh-Plesset problems are also explored, yielding novel, analytically solvable equations that can be compared with ongoing and future experiments on gravitational effects on fluid dynamics. The relationship between a cell's phenotype and the proteins it contains is highly complex,  despite the significant progress made in recent years in using proteomic data to classify cells and identify the drivers of their phenotype.  A key challenge in this area is modeling the interactions between large numbers of proteins, which typically requires simplifying assumptions or a massive amount of data.  In this work, we developed an approach that uses a compact representation of the proteome to capture the functional relationships between proteins and applies it to a comprehensive set of 300 cellular traits.  Our approach, which is based on a combination of the proteins in each cellular compartment and the proteins that interact with each other, accurately predicts the effects of mutations in the genes that encode these proteome components.  We found that the influence of a protein's sequence on the phenotype-associated SNPs associated with it is a key factor in our approach, which we validated using multiple types of data, including large-scale functional screens, in vitro experiments, and in vivo experiments.  Our approach also enabled us to identify new drivers of cellular traits and predict their experimental validation rates.  Overall, our work shows that it is possible to model the proteome in a compact and meaningful way that reflects its functional properties and can be used to predict the effects of mutations in the genes that encode its components.  Our approach can be applied to any organism for which there is a comprehensive set of proteomic data available, which includes many important human diseases. To further investigate this phenomenon, ALICE has observed the production of KS0 and (Λ+¯Λ-) pairs in mid-central 13 TeV proton-proton collisions at 7.98 TeV and 5.02 TeV, respectively. In particular, the threshold for particle pair formation was determined to be around 0.45 GeV/c^2 at 7.98 TeV and 0.40 GeV/c^2 at 5.02 TeV. This new method is tested on a sample of 11 local dwarf spheroidal galaxy candidates from the Pan-STARRS1 survey that have limited line velocity data for several stars within each candidate. The researchers compared their results to more accurate measurements obtained for 5 of these candidates with a larger number of line velocity measurements. The new method was also assessed for its accuracy in determining the line velocity dispersion and rotation velocity parameters. The results showed that the new approach provides more accurate line velocity dispersion and rotation velocity measurements than previous methods, especially when only a limited number of line velocity measurements are available for a given star. Human conversational engagements seamlessly integrate varied meanings and facts, which serves as a foundation for a compelling theory of mind. Yet, current natural language generation models, despite their ability to produce engaging text, tend to prioritize form over content and often struggle with diverse responses. In our work, we aim to develop a method to enhance the semantic diversity of models during generation, which can be achieved by fine-tuning the model on diverse descriptions of shared images in a dual setting. Automated driving systems rely heavily on video data and can function effectively even in areas where wireless connectivity is limited. To support these systems in diverse, ever-changing scenarios, it is essential to develop more robust perception modules. Online action recognition models, in particular, need to be capable of adapting to new situations and predicting future actions based on past behavior. However, current approaches often prioritize prediction accuracy over computational efficiency and real-time performance. To address this limitation, we propose a novel efficient framework, dubbed EfficientOnlineActionPredictor (EOAP), which leverages an attention-based encoder and a lightweight decoder utilizing bidirectional recurrent modules. To further enhance performance without incurring significant computational overhead, we introduce an attention-based temporal modeling approach. By incorporating an attention mechanism, our framework optimizes EOAP's latency-per-data-point to 13.6 ms on a single GPU, outperforming state-of-the-art online action recognition models by 11.6%. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of EOAP, achieving a precision of 0.83 at a latency of 13.6 ms and achieving a precision of 0.92 at a latency of 33.9 ms. Moreover, we demonstrate EOAP's capability to accurately predict driving maneuvers on the NADA dataset, ultimately contributing a high-performance, real-time online action recognition model suitable for large-scale driving datasets. For objects that burn hydrogen in stars below 0.6 solar masses, there is a critical limit beyond which angular momentum prevents the onset of sustained hydrogen combustion in the center via the Kelvin-Helmholtz mechanism. Exceeding the angular momentum threshold results in objects that exclusively experience binary interaction-driven hydrogen ignition. This ignition occurs either directly within the star or within a surrounding disk, and is closely linked to the formation of a fossil planetary system. Objects that surpass the angular momentum threshold that marks the onset of binary interaction-driven hydrogen ignition are predicted to possess detectable signs in the H-alpha spectral line, specifically in ultra-cool dwarfs and brown dwarfs that exhibit low surface temperatures. Notably, this scenario is exemplified by the H-alpha emission stars LHS 2520B and LHS 3375B, which are low-mass, binary white dwarf systems with extremely short orbital periods. These objects are also notable for exhibiting the highest angular momentum known among hydrogen-burning objects, and they offer a unique opportunity to study the effects of high angular momentum on binary white dwarfs that have evolved from low-mass hydrogen-burning precursors. Using extensive numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the high angular momentum in these binary systems results in significant tidal interactions that cause substantial mass redistribution between the two components, leading to enhanced thermal and chemical mixing that accelerates the cooling process. As a result, we find that these binary white dwarfs exhibit cooling curves that are shifted to shorter ages compared to their cooling counterparts with lower angular momentum. Consequently, we find that the high angular momentum in these binary systems results in a 10-20% increase in thermal energy dissipation, which is sufficient to account for the observed H-alpha emission. Furthermore, we estimate that the total luminosity contributed by the thermalized tidal energy in these binary systems is equivalent to approximately 10% of the total X-ray and extreme ultraviolet emission observed in ultra-cool dwarfs and brown dwarfs that exhibit low surface temperatures. Lastly, we anticipate that a substantial portion of these objects are associated with binary systems that have experienced hydrogen ignition in a surrounding disk or within the star itself, and that they can be identified through their H-alpha emission. In this context, we propose that the detection of this emission can serve as a binary system's signature, providing a large sample of binary hydrogen-burning objects with high angular momentum that can be studied in detail. Moreover, we present a new approach to calculating the minimum k requirement and examine how this method compares to existing techniques. Deep learning models often employ optimization techniques and regularization methods to enhance performance, but employing score calibration methods can provide an alternative boost in accuracy across various classes. Our study investigates the effect of score calibration on deep learning models dealing with class imbalance and assesses the impact on performance. We initially examine the relationship between misclassification loss and the distance between samples, followed by an analysis of how the degree of imbalance affects performance. We then present numerical and graphical evidence highlighting the benefits of score calibration in improving performance for underrepresented classes. Moreover, we develop an intuitive explanation for its effectiveness in tackling class imbalance issues. We also introduce a novel framework that enables the derivation of bounds on the reduction in error rates achievable through score calibration. This framework enables us to create a new algorithm to determine the optimal regularization parameter for reduced error rates. We provide theoretical guarantees and supporting empirical evidence for our findings. All code and data used in this study are available online.

We demonstrate that when the underlying field of a power series field is infinite, decidability of the theory of the power series field, augmented by a total residue map, holds true. This finding contradicts a previously held conjecture. Additionally, we prove that over a finite field, the power series field does not possess a total residue map whose associated geometry is valid. This result supports a decision procedure for the power series field over an infinite field, as it implies the ability to decide validity of statements within the power series field itself. We also establish that validity in the ring of power series, as opposed to the field of power series, can be determined through a decision procedure derived from the method used for the power series field. Furthermore, we demonstrate that decidability of the geometry associated with the algebraic closure of the ring of polynomials in one variable also holds true. This result extends on previous research conducted by Denef and Lipshitz. Lastly, we explore the implications of our findings on the geometry associated with valuated matroids. We conclude by highlighting the potential for our methods to contribute to research on the geometry of ordered abelian groups and their associated modules. This knowledge may, in turn, aid in resolving the long-standing question regarding the decidability of the theory of ordered abelian groups. This paper is based on chapters from the Ph.D. theses of P. H. H. Heckmann and T. J. H. Vickers.

The efficacy of Flush+Reload attacks, a technique used to identify memory leaks, can be enhanced through the use of HyperThreading Technology (HyperDegrade). By applying HyperDegrade, a single core is capable of performing two core functions: one utilizing the original Flush+Reload approach and the other using a new technique where a thread monitors memory access patterns following a flush operation. By leveraging this capability, the time required for successful identification of memory leaks is reduced from minutes to milliseconds, and the number of necessary scans is decreased from hundreds to just one. Moreover, HyperDegrade enables detection of various types of memory including stack and heap memory, in addition to implicit memory, and introduces a new attack that identifies memory usage based on access patterns following a flush operation. A demonstration of the effectiveness of HyperDegrade is provided through the use of several examples, including the exploitation of vulnerabilities in widely used applications such as libpng, libtiff, and libjpeg-turbo. The findings of this research highlight the limitations of current hypervisor-based detection methods and emphasize the significance of mitigating side-channel leaks in software development. The associated proof-of-concept code is available online. The minimal supersymmetric standard model with three neutrino species and a small Dirac neutrino mass is examined in the context of the Higgs mass and the stability of dark stars. It is determined that both stable white dwarfs and neutron stars require at least one of the three mass states of the Higgs boson to be greater than 125 GeV or one of the three mass states of the Higgs boson to be smaller than 123 GeV, assuming it can be directly measured. Additionally, if the lightest neutrino mass in the model is very small, it must be approximately equal to zero, as indicated by recent short-baseline neutrino experiments, in order for the most dense dark stars to be stable against neutron emission or neutrino loss in the supersymmetric standard model. However, if the lightest neutrino mass is substantial, even the most dense dark stars can remain stable with the minimal supersymmetric standard model parameters.
