Mathematical models of disease dynamics, particularly those described by differential equations, have been extensively developed for modeling infectious disease spread. However, the numerous model parameters pose a challenge for forecasting disease progression. To address this challenge, researchers employ fitting methods using available data to estimate model parameters, which are then used to predict future outcomes. Specifically, Bayesian methods have been employed for this estimation, utilizing prior knowledge to constrain the possible solutions. However, these methods are only effective if the model's biological plausibility is considered during the estimation process. We propose an alternative approach, which involves first identifying the set of model parameters that fit the available data and also adhere to the defined biological feasibility criteria. This approach is referred to as infeasibility traversal. We demonstrate this approach using a well-established model of disease dynamics, the SEIR model, and illustrate its application using data from the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany. We also compare our results with those obtained using traditional Bayesian estimation methods. Our findings indicate that the model parameters estimated through infeasibility traversal, while fitting the observed data, exhibit a different distribution and are more dispersed than those estimated using Bayesian methods. Notably, the models obtained through infeasibility traversal exhibit a higher likelihood than those estimated through Bayesian methods, indicating that the former are more consistent with the data. We also observe that the models meeting the biological feasibility criteria, as identified through infeasibility traversal, are more dispersed in terms of their ability to fit the data, with some models over or underestimating the actual disease spread. However, the models that do not meet the biological feasibility criteria, as identified through infeasibility traversal, result in even poorer predictions, with some models exhibiting unbounded behavior and others failing to capture the disease spread dynamics. Overall, our findings highlight the significance of considering biological feasibility when fitting differential models to data, as this approach identifies a subset of models that fit the data reasonably well, as well as models that fail to capture the observed disease spread dynamics due to either over or underestimation. This approach can be particularly valuable for forecasting disease spread based on limited data, as it constrains the possible solutions to a manageable set of models that adhere to the defined biological feasibility criteria. We believe that this approach can be applied to a broader range of modeling problems involving differential equations. Additionally, we propose an open-source software package, available on GitHub, which utilizes the open-source software package Dune-Agds for spatial differential equation solutions and provides a user-friendly interface for infeasibility traversal through the Shiny web framework

Acronyms are abbreviations created from initial parts of phrases or sentences, commonly used in written language to represent lengthy concepts or phrases. They are employed across various domains, including business, science, technology, and healthcare, serving as company identifiers, technical terminology, and medical terminology. The rise of text-based applications necessitates the ability to automatically identify and clarify unfamiliar acronyms encountered in text. This task is complicated by the vast number of possible acronym meanings, which are not systematically organized, forcing systems to rely on general language understanding to effectively handle them. This work introduces a novel approach to building systems capable of identifying and resolving acronym ambiguities across multiple domains and presents a new dataset, called Acronym-Entailment-Graphs (AEG), which contains a comprehensive set of acronym-based triples, extracted from Wikipedia, comprising 10,000+ entities with 200,000+ triples. This dataset enables systems to evaluate their performance in identifying and resolving acronym ambiguities. Experimental results using this dataset reveal that incorporating domain information through an attention-based model enhances the accuracy of both acronym identification and entailment tasks. This work also explores the application of these systems to other abbreviation types and investigates the characteristics of effective acronym descriptions. The developed system is available online for further research and community utilization. The research on acronym processing is in its infancy, and this work aims to stimulate interest in this area to address the challenges posed by increasingly complex and domain-dominant acronyms. The work is relevant to the community working on named entity recognition, word sense induction, and the processing of technical language. Researchers have successfully created long-lived atom-molecule correlations in gas states using a technique called Feshbach resonance. To analyze complex quantum processes involving multiple bodies, researchers use simplified models that capture essential dynamics while discarding less important details. In a recent study, a non-rigid pendulum model was found to accurately describe the interaction between atoms and molecules in Feshbach resonance experiments. In this model, the pendulum's length represents the atom-molecule interaction and is influenced by two opposing forces: the stiffness of molecular bonds pulling the pendulum tight and the potential energy for an atom to become a molecule, which extends the pendulum. In an atomic gas, multiple pendulums move independently, their movements affected by collisions that cause the pendulums to swing in sync. In an earlier paper, the researchers found that by mimicking the pendulums' behavior, they could reproduce the onset of molecule-atom oscillations and the pendulums' synchronization leading to instability. In this follow-up work, the non-rigid pendulum model was validated using a different method and its phases analyzed to show that the pendulums' synchronization occurs when the atomic gas' temperature matches the energy of an energy gap created during the Feshbach resonance process. The model was also used to identify the potential for quantum phase slips in atom-molecule systems. Notably, the non-rigid pendulum model has a broader application in physics, as it can represent the interaction between vortices in superfluids and the environment. The model was tested using a quantum simulation technique called digital quantum annealing, in which the atom-molecule gap was recreated by gradually decreasing the energy of the system. In this process, the gap's width was found to be influenced by the vortices' motion and their interaction with the pendulum representing the superfluid's environment. The results indicate that the nodal lines in ZrTeP contribute significantly to the anomalous Hall effect (AHE), with the anomalous contribution to the Hall effect being dominated by the nodal lines. This advanced method, built with deep learning, surpasses previous benchmarks by classifying and accurately outlining four diverse brain tumor types, along with segmenting five organs within abdominal and chest regions. To enhance hydroacoustic survey efficiency and reduce costs, a new method called Principal Component Geostatistical Analysis (PCGA) has been developed to estimate riverbed bathymetry using limited flow velocity measurements. By leveraging spatial statistics and the information contained in flow velocity data, PCGA can pinpoint and prioritize areas for further measurement, enabling a complete bathymetric map with a reduced number of measurements. To test PCGA's effectiveness, a series of controlled experiments were conducted using a tank and a river with varying levels of sediment complexity. In the tank experiments, PCGA was able to create accurate 3D models of the bed topography using just 5-10% of the total number of measurements required for traditional methods. In the river experiments, PCGA performed well in areas with minimal vegetation and sand bars, but its performance degraded in areas with dense vegetation and complex sand bars. To address these challenges, enhancements to the PCGA algorithm were made, including the use of a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method to account for non-Gaussian data distributions. With these modifications, the algorithm was able to accurately estimate topography in areas with dense vegetation and complex sand bars using a larger number of localized measurements. To apply PCGA in real-world scenarios, a Python implementation of the algorithm was created, along with a graphical user interface called PCGA-GUI, which allows users to prioritize areas for measurement based on previous surveys. To demonstrate PCGA-GUI's capabilities, a case study was conducted on the Mississippi River, where the algorithm successfully identified areas for further measurement that led to significant improvements in the overall accuracy of the bathymetric map. Overall, PCGA and PCGA-GUI offer a promising approach to enhancing hydroacoustic survey efficiency and reducing costs. To facilitate further development and testing of PCGA, the algorithm's source code has been made publicly available on GitHub. As the algorithm continues to evolve, its potential applications extend beyond hydroacoustic surveys to other inverse problems involving geophysical measurements. Futhermore, the PCGA algorithm can be adapted to other numerical methods such as level set methods to improve its performance. To facilitate this, the code has been written in a modular format that allows for easy substitution of different numerical methods. To test PCGA's robustness, the algorithm was run with a range of parameters, including different flow velocity models, spatial correlation lengths, and initial estimates of the bed topography. The results showed that PCGA was able to produce accurate estimates of the bed topography even with unrealistic parameters

Creating High Dynamic Range (HDR) images from multiple exposures requires selecting the optimal exposure settings. Current automated methods choose exposure settings through machine learning by analyzing a large dataset of labeled images. These approaches assume access to vast datasets containing detailed information about the labeling process. This study challenges this assumption by investigating methods to choose optimal exposure settings using minimal human input for learning. The proposed approach, based on the Kronecker product factorization of the HDR imaging matrix, significantly reduces the need for labeled data. The introduced low-rank factorization model learns the minimal human input data efficiently and is applied to HDR image reconstruction from a small set of images with varying exposures. The results show that the proposed approach, learned with only a small set of labeled images, outperforms state-of-the-art deep learning methods using large datasets containing detailed labeling information. Furthermore, the method learns exposure settings that generalize across different scenes and scenes with moving objects, outperforming methods that learn exposure settings for each HDR image individually. The proposed approach was further validated through a user study, demonstrating that the generated HDR images are preferred over those created using state-of-the-art deep learning methods. The code and data are available at https://github.com/paragk/HDR-kronecker.

We establish a generalization of the Madsen-Weiss theorem by linking the b-principle to stable splittings of classifying spaces. This generalized framework is grounded in the concepts of the b-principle and stability theorems, and is then utilized to derive novel applications, including proofs of specific cases of the Madsen-Weiss theorem. Futhermore, we demonstrate the value of this approach in identifying potential proofs for other instances of the Madsen-Weiss theorem. The associated obstructions are computed using the known parametrizations of the spaces involved, obtained from the standard construction of classifying spaces via Postnikov towers. The general methodology we employ is then illustrated through a specific example related to the Madsen-Weiss theorem. The example in question concerns the $G$-equivariant structure set of surgery spaces for extended orbifolds of type $(2,1)$, where the group $G$ is a product of a finite group and the fundamental group of a surface. These settings often involve visual elements accompanied by scripted dialogue, and the soundtracks are carefully selected to resonate with the target audience, influencing their voting behavior. However, the lack of well-designed evaluation metrics hinders the development of music generation systems tailored to specific purposes, such as enhancing the viewing experience of persuasive videos. Overall, our research demonstrated the effectiveness of music generation in enhancing the viewing experience of persuasive videos and identified areas for further exploration in the field. Neural network-based safety, crucial for reliable human interaction and interoperability, hinges on thoroughly understood decision-making processes. Researchers initially employed the term "explainability" to describe this requirement, but it has been increasingly recognized as distinct from the public's desire for intuitive understanding. To progress in this area, it is essential to develop a standardized measure for comparing the similarity of neural networks using gradient-based assessments. Currently, the field of neural network-based safety is fragmented due to the absence of a unified framework for quantifying and evaluating safety properties. To address this issue, we propose SafetyGauge, an extensive framework consisting of precisely defined metrics and evaluation tools to quantify and assess various safety aspects of neural networks. Specifically, we introduce measures for quantifying defense mechanisms, such as determining the percentage of gradients that are correctly predicted by a neural network with masked connections. Additionally, SafetyGauge encompasses multiple evaluation techniques, including the utilization of formal verification tools and the creation of customized evaluation frameworks. To illustrate the capabilities of SafetyGauge, we conducted a comprehensive comparison of various neural network architectures using a range of attributes, including those involving complex gradient-based assessments. The results of our comparison reveal that both straightforward evaluations and more intricate assessments yield valuable insights into the functioning and behavior of neural networks, ultimately contributing to the advancement of neural network safety through rigorous analysis and comparison. The framework we present is publicly accessible at https://safetygauges.github.io/.

The successful creation of acoustic metamaterials at the microscale relies on a thorough comprehension of fluid viscosity's impact. A comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that incorporates thermal properties and accounts for the dispersion relationship $\eta \lambda/U^2$ in all fluid-dynamic interactions is required to accurately model this phenomenon. By implementing this theory in a finite-element method based on Boltzmann's hydrodynamic equations, we can simulate complex fluid-metal interactions in acoustic metamaterials and solve the Maxwell equations to analyze the electromagnetic fields generated. This approach enables us to simulate an optical trap and calculate the force exerted on a microdisk consisting of various materials, including gold, silver, and polymer, when exposed to Gaussian beams of different wavelengths. Notably, when the laser wavelength is comparable to the hydrodynamic skin depth, significant long-range interactions arise, leading to unexpected force patterns that can be manipulated by adjusting the fluid's temperature or the microdisk's thickness. This research offers a new framework for understanding the interplay between light, acoustic vibrations, and fluid viscosity and may lead to innovative strategies for controlling acoustic vibrations using light and microscale devices that leverage long-range interactions. These findings could also contribute to the development of novel light-driven acoustic sensors and actuators, providing a crucial step towards realizing the full potential of acoustic metamaterials in microscale applications. The concept of external chattering behavior in control systems is formally defined as a recurring oscillation between two distinct trajectories caused by unbounded control inputs. We demonstrate that this chattering phenomenon is inherent in control systems driven by unbounded controls, and provide a lower bound on the dimension of their attractors. Additionally, we establish conditions under which the chattering behavior is localized within a specific, higher-dimensional space outside the bounded regime. This result is achieved through the application of control-theoretic frameworks and the use of an external hyperbolicity approach, allowing us to analyze systems driven by unbounded controls while focusing on the long-term dynamics influenced by these controls. We also illustrate our findings with an example involving a linear system and an oscillatory control input. Furthermore, we derive a condition for non-chattering behavior in systems driven by bounded controls, and this condition is analogous to those previously established for the finite-dimensional case. Moreover, we explore the relationship between our definition of external chattering and other, more general definitions, and discuss the implications of our results within the context of recent research. Finally, we address potential future directions for this area of study. 

Keywords: control systems, chattering behavior, unbounded controls, external chattering, high-dimensional attractors.

Deep neural network-based classifiers have revolutionized the field of computer vision by achieving exceptional accuracy and efficiency in various tasks. Nevertheless, traditional deep neural networks are inherently prone to overfitting and require substantial amounts of data to avoid significant errors. Expert human annotators are still the primary source for data annotation in various tasks, including object detection and segmentation, despite being both costly and time-consuming. Even with high-confidence predictions from modern deep neural networks, correcting these mistakes is essential to ensure data quality. Consequently, an efficient method is urgently needed to develop a system capable of generating diverse, high-quality annotated data with minimal human intervention. To tackle this challenge, we present a novel technique called diverse pseudo-labeling, which incorporates an efficient thresholding method to filter pseudo-labels of varying quality for iterative refinement. By leveraging efficient neural networks and pseudo-labeling, we developed a diverse pseudo-labeling framework that effectively generates a wide range of high-quality annotated data with minimal human oversight. Experimental results on popular benchmarks, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet, demonstrate that our method yields superior performance compared to conventional pseudo-labeling techniques, especially in scenarios with limited human annotation. Notably, our diverse pseudo-labeling approach achieves a notable 4.8% improvement in accuracy on ImageNet, outperforming the current state-of-the-art method. Moreover, our technique is remarkably cost-effective, with a significant reduction in the number of human annotations required, amounting to $0.01 per annotation on ImageNet. To fairly assess reinforcement learning algorithms, it is essential to develop a standardized evaluation framework that gradually introduces new elements into a stable environment. We introduce a new metric called relative difference in value (RDV) to gauge the impact of curriculum changes on an agent's performance. RDV is calculated as the difference between an agent's average rewards in two distinct curriculum phases, divided by the maximum possible rewards in the more challenging phase. We argue that a desirable evaluation algorithm should exhibit an RDV close to zero, indicating minimal decline in performance as the curriculum becomes increasingly difficult. We also explore alternative evaluation frameworks that incorporate multiple agents and curriculum phases to control for the degree of difficulty. Furthermore, we apply these methods to evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art reinforcement learning algorithms on three complex tasks, finding that some algorithms appear to perform better according to our criteria than in previous studies. Our results suggest that a rigorous evaluation process that accounts for the degree of difficulty in curriculum design can provide a more accurate assessment of an algorithm's capabilities. This approach ensures that the solution is feasible and adheres to the rules defined by the initial and final DCR graphs. We also introduce a metric to evaluate the quality of the process path by calculating the f-score for each graph along the timeline. Building on our previous work, this paper expands on the concepts introduced in [6] and [7] concerning integer subsets with restricted sums that generate dense sequences in arithmetic progressions. Specifically, we investigate the scenario where a bounded number of summands is allowed. This results in the density of generated sequences increasing within a broader range, characterized by exponential bounds, in place of the quadratic bounds observed in the unbounded summands case. The minimum density threshold required is directly proportional to the square of the lowest number of summands permitted. Moreover, this relationship remains optimal, both in terms of the density of sequences generated and the implied exponential relationship. Current deep learning models used for Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) are limited by their reliance on expensive exhaustive matching processes, which hinders their scalability and hindering their potential for real-world applications. To overcome this limitation, our research introduces Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), a technique that selectively eliminates unnecessary proposals during training, thereby speeding up training by a factor of nearly five while maintaining comparable performance to exhaustive methods. Furthermore, BNPS speeds up inference by an average of 1.5 times without compromising accuracy when applied to fully trained models. We demonstrate the efficacy of BNPS across multiple popular VRD models and datasets, showcasing its universal applicability. Moreover, an in-depth analysis of BNPS is provided, which reveals that BNPS enhances model generalizability by reducing the risk of overfitting and promoting the discovery of shared features across diverse proposals. Ultimately, our research indicates that BNPS represents a pivotal optimization technique for VRD models, which can be employed during both training and inference to achieve substantial gains in efficiency without sacrificing accuracy. The code and models are openly accessible at https://github.com/leiming1999/BNPS.

The success of human action recognition using deep learning techniques relies heavily on large, high-quality datasets. However, such datasets are often limited in size, leading to significant disparities between real-world data and training data error rates. This study introduces an unsupervised active learning framework that prioritizes limited-labeling real-world data for the remaining training data, resulting in the greatest reduction in the error rate. The framework utilizes an encoder-decoder model that leverages mutual information maximization and incorporates attention mechanisms to focus on action-relevant data features. Our experiments conducted on three diverse datasets demonstrate the proposed method's effectiveness in selecting the most informative real-world data for additional labeling, resulting in a substantial decrease in error rates of up to 15.6% with only 1-5 additional labels per selected sample. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/AL-SUP.

The formation of galaxies is characterized by the accretion of gas, stars, and dark matter, which leads to complex interactions and a diverse range of outcomes. Using high-resolution N-body and gas-particle simulations, our research focuses on the early development of a massive galaxy, specifically within the first billion years, as it undergoes significant structural transformations. Initially, the galaxy forms through the merger of smaller halos, resulting in a compact, rapidly rotating disk with a distinct bulge. However, as more halos accrete and merge with the galaxy, its structure evolves in response, with the development of a massive, bulge-dominated core surrounded by a slowly rotating, disk-like system, and a prominent, long-lived ring feature. A comparison with a similar simulation without star formation reveals that the conversion of gas into stars has slowed the core's growth, causing a more rapid development of the outer disk. Furthermore, an examination of the galaxy's satellite population reveals that the accretion of individual satellites contributes a significant proportion of its mass, with a preference for merging with the galaxy's core, and a notable enhancement of the galaxy's core during its first billion years of growth, with a mass fraction increasing from 10% to 50%. The simulation also shows that the accretion of satellites leads to a series of minor mergers, resulting in the creation of extended, star-studded tails, as well as a network of collisionless streams that influence the galaxy's potential, and shape its overall morphology. These findings highlight the significant role that the accretion of gas, stars, and dark matter, and the mergers of these components, play in the complex structural evolution of galaxies, and emphasize the importance of incorporating these processes in simulations of galaxy formation. Additionally, our research provides a framework for predicting the galaxy's mass assembly history, and its structural and morphological development, based on its mass and redshift, and a set of model parameters that account for the galaxy's star formation history, and its interactions with its surroundings. This approach enables a statistical analysis of the galaxy's structural evolution, and allows for a comparison with observations, and a testing of the model's predictions against observations of real galaxies. Our research also enables a comparison of our model's predictions with those of other simulations, and a consideration of the role of assumptions, such as the inclusion of gas in the simulations, and the level of resolution, in shaping the galaxy's structure. Finally, our research provides a foundation for a greater understanding of the complex interactions that govern the galaxy

A well-trained neural model can efficiently generate programs, but its effectiveness depends on high-quality training data. However, ensuring the correctness of such programs also requires verifying their safety properties. In this study, we investigate an alternative approach, using a static program analyzer that provides weak supervision from safety verification to strengthen a neural model. We designed an experiment where we trained a neural program generator using a static analyzer that checks for array-index bounds and pointer safety. The analyzer only works for a limited set of programs, thus representing weak supervision. We found that this approach significantly improved the safety of programs generated by the neural model, even when verified using a more comprehensive static analyzer. This suggests that combining strong supervision (i.e., extensive testing) with weak supervision (i.e., safety verification) can lead to substantial gains in program safety. Notably, programs that passed weak supervision had a 200-fold higher chance of being safe when subjected to strong supervision. This implies that safety-enhanced neural program generators could be useful in situations where full-scale verification is impractical, such as in online program generation. Moreover, this approach may be applied to other domains and problems where strong and weak supervision have different formats. As an example, we successfully applied this technique to a neural model that converts SQL queries to Java, using a static analyzer that checks for data integrity and ensures query validity. One of the largest geomagnetic storms in recent history occurred on November 7th, 2004, when a massive geomagnetic disturbance reached a Kp level of 8.7. This event was triggered by a sudden geomagnetic surge caused by a coronair mass ejection observed from space. Researchers studied the effects of this event on the upper atmosphere at low latitudes, specifically in the region near India, by analyzing data from the ROSES (Rocket-borne Spectrograph for Emissions from the Sun) instrument launched from Sriharikota, India. Although the instrument was designed to study the Sun's spectral lines from space, it was not designed to withstand the extreme conditions of a geomagnetic storm of this magnitude. As such, the instrument experienced significant damage, including a temperature increase of over 10 degrees Celsius and a shift in its spatial orientation of over 1000 degrees. Despite this, the data collected during the event showed the effects of the geomagnetic surge on the upper atmosphere, including an unexpected increase in the instrument's altitude of over 100 km and a delay of several minutes in its data transmission. The data also revealed the presence of a new spectral line in the instrument's data, which was not present in pre-storm data. The research team believes that this new spectral line may be related to the instrument's exposure to the intense radiation during the geomagnetic storm. The incident provided valuable insights into the design and operation of space instruments, particularly those launched from low-latitude launch sites, and highlighted the need for instruments to be designed with the ability to withstand extreme conditions during launch and in space. The research also demonstrated the importance of conducting thorough tests of instruments before launch, particularly in situations like the recent SpaceX TMF (Transition Module Flight) test, which resulted in the loss of multiple Starlink satellites due to a failure of the TMF module to withstand the forces of launch. The research team is working with the SpaceX team to investigate the incident and identify lessons that can be applied to future SpaceX missions. The research also sparked a new area of research into the effects of geomagnetic storms on upper atmosphere dynamics and the potential for instruments to provide valuable insights into these events. The research team is planning to launch a new set of instruments from the same launch site in 2024 to study the effects of geomagnetic storms in more detail. We introduce an efficient, incremental, and high-precision anomaly detection framework based on an adaptive one-dimensional autoencoder (A1DAE) model. This approach uses an adaptive single-dimensional encoding layer to generate a single summary score for each data sample, eliminating the need for additional neighbors during the encoding process. A1DAE incorporates a dynamic neighborhood size that adapts to each data point's density, enabling it to effectively detect anomalies without predefined parameters. Building on this, we developed an incremental anomaly detection method that updates the model in real-time for new data arrivals while gradually adjusting the neighborhood size based on accumulating data. Both the single-step and incremental implementations of A1DAE outperformed traditional methods such as Local Outlier Factor (LOF) and One-Class SVM on multiple real-world datasets. Furthermore, the incremental A1DAE exhibited comparable performance to the single-step A1DAE after sufficient updates, with a significant reduction in computational costs. A1DAE was found to be particularly effective in low-dimensional data with dense regions, while its incremental version performed well in datasets with varying densities. A1DAE's code is openly available on https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/A1DAE. All datasets employed in this research are accessible on https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q. Additionally, the paper is accompanied by an accompanying video that can be accessed on https://youtu.be/zhengyuanwu.

This encryption variant meets the requirements for a strong encryption standard, known as indistinguishable encryption (IND-CPA security). We also create an encryption protocol that can securely handle multiple users with different denial risks in mind, referred to as a multi-user setting. These cryptographic tools are useful for preventing the misuse of government power, which can force people to reveal information through court orders. We examine the consequences of using a coherent state with a random phase in quantum key distribution over long distances, specifically in the context of the Michelson Interferometer (MDI) configuration. Our analysis extends the original proposal by Lo et al. and includes various implementation variations, such as applying linear channel loss, beam splitter with less than equal port weights, and phase voltage errors in the interferometer, all modeled with realistic parameters. These scenarios are simulated through realistic simulations and the resulting data is used to evaluate the performance of different protocols, assessing efficiency through gain, error rate, and final key rate metrics. Furthermore, the optimal parameters for implementing the conjugate encoding protocol effectively are determined and analyzed. Finally, implementing the conjugate encoding protocol over long distances is shown to be beneficial for achieving high-security levels. Although the variance of the vacuum state used increases with distance, the gain and error rate used to calculate the final key rate exhibit distinct behaviors with respect to distance. As a result, the conjugate encoding protocol offers enhanced security without incurring significant variance penalties. Consequently, it is particularly well-suited for generating highly secure keys over extended distances. This study proves the existence of a PTAS for the minimization of general-valued CSPs under two specific conditions: when the variables can be ordered in a way that restricts the possible values for each variable as the assignment progresses and when the variables can be ordered in a way that restricts the possible constraints for each variable as the assignment progresses. Two new techniques were developed to achieve this PTAS: an iterative process of approximating and refining local optima and a way of solving restricted subproblems efficiently. This research also provides a lower bound on the number of variables that must be assigned before a PTAS is guaranteed to work, showing that for some cases, a PTAS may not be possible unless NP is not equal to NP. Advancements in medical image analysis using deep learning have led to significant breakthroughs in the past decade. The evaluation process resulted in the top-scoring five methods being selected, which were then subjected to a series of rigorous assessments, including quantitative performance metrics, robustness testing, and surveys among medical professionals. The outcome of this evaluation, which included a selected top-scoring methods, was thoroughly examined and the results presented at the challenge's final demonstration session held during MICCAI 2021. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the Med-XAI Grand Challenge, which includes the motivation, evaluation process, results, and the outcome of the challenge. Pre-training models using knowledge graphs consisting of factual triples has been a prominent strategy in natural language processing. Unlike traditional text-based data, knowledge graphs reduce the reliance on language patterns seen in vast amounts of text. Recent studies have shown that models pre-trained on knowledge graphs perform well in question-answering tasks, often surpassing those trained on vast amounts of text. However, these studies have limitations, as they used small-scale knowledge graphs and didn't account for knowledge graph construction methods used by the pre-training models. In our research, we compare models pre-trained on large-scale knowledge graphs to those pre-trained on traditional text-based data, evaluating their performance in question-answering tasks. We also analyze factors affecting the quality of knowledge graphs and their impact on models' performance. Our results indicate that models pre-trained on knowledge graphs outperform those trained on text-based data in many cases, but there's still room for improvement, especially when it comes to relation classification. We've made our data and experiments publicly available, contributing valuable resources for researchers exploring the intersection of natural language processing and knowledge graphs. This study investigates recent nonlocal diffusion models, which have been employed to model image processing, and examines how they relate to traditional classical PDE models as the nonlocal interaction kernel exhibits local characteristics. We introduce a new approach to approximate nonlocal PDEs by classical PDEs and develop an equation representation that combines nonlocal and classical operators. This combined framework enables the inclusion of widely used nonlocal and classical PDE models, such as Cahn-Hilliard, Allen-Cahn, Korteveg-de Vries, and heat equations. We then investigate the theoretical properties of the proposed framework, including existence and uniqueness of solutions, energy identities, and bound estimates. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the nonlocal and classical kernel parameters and derive an optimal parameter configuration for approximation. This study is supported by numerical experiments and potential applications to the development of efficient numerical methods for nonlocal PDEs. Ultimately, the proposed framework provides valuable insights into the fundamental connections between nonlocal and classical PDE models.

This paper builds on our earlier work concerning the degenerate Eisenstein series formed by the action of a Weyl group coset, expanding our initial results to cover cases where the coset's irreducible representation is non-trivial. Specifically, we derive an explicit formula for the degenerate Eisenstein series' Fourier coefficient in a specific basis, and confirm that the obtained result aligns with general coefficient norm estimates proposed by J. Miller and C. D. Sorensen. Moreover, we establish a direct relationship between the coefficients of two distinct degenerate Eisenstein series, employing this connection to demonstrate the equipartition of the coefficients' norms. Finally, we present a novel proof for the coset's invariance property of the degenerate Eisenstein series' norm, initially conjectured by H. Jakobitz and S. J. Miller. This proof relies on our derived coefficient formula and related geometric transformations. Consequently, we demonstrate the coincidence of the coefficients with a specific class of non-degenerate Eisenstein series, whose residue field values are directly linked to the coefficients' norms, thereby establishing their equipartition. This equipartition is further shown to imply the geometrically anticipated norm normalization for the coset itself. This finding is extendable to a broader context, encompassing extensions of the special linear group over local fields and certain adelic extensions. This research is grounded in our previous joint work with H. Jakobitz and S. J. Miller.

A novel algorithm for generating font glyphs is introduced, which prioritizes the aesthetic rendering of line joins in fonts. Most digital fonts rely on the "brush font" technique to produce distinctive endings for lines, but this method is computationally intensive when applied to complex glyphs. In contrast, the "brush font" technique can result in unrealistic line connections, particularly with "M" and "N" characters, which have non-linear connections. To address this issue, a new algorithm was developed to naturally render line connections in any font type. This algorithm creates natural-looking connections by analyzing the shape of a glyph and identifying its edges, then it uses a mathematical formula to determine the most natural-looking line connections. The algorithm can produce high-quality results with minimal computational overhead, and it can be applied to any font type regardless of its complexity. In experiments, the algorithm showed a significant improvement in line connections, especially for "M" and "N" characters, and it outperformed other algorithms in terms of accuracy. In terms of performance, the algorithm was comparable to other algorithms, but it had a lower computational overhead. In terms of perception, human subjects preferred the results produced by the algorithm, and it was able to produce results in a fraction of the time required by other algorithms. The algorithm was also applied to various fonts and it was found that it can produce high-quality results with minimal adjustments, and it can be used to improve the aesthetic quality of line connections in any font type. The algorithm was also found to be robust and it can handle complex glyphs with non-linear connections. In terms of future work, the algorithm can be further improved by incorporating other aesthetic preferences, and it can be applied to other areas such as graphic design and engineering. The algorithm was tested on a dataset of 1,000 glyphs and it produced an accuracy of 95%, which is comparable to other algorithms. The algorithm has a computational overhead of 0.1 seconds per glyph, which is lower than other algorithms. The algorithm was found to prefer line connections that are 1.5 times the width of the stroke, which is consistent with human preferences. The algorithm can produce high-quality results with a stroke width of 0.1-1.0 pixels, which covers the typical range of stroke widths used in fonts. The algorithm was found to perform well with a dataset of 500 glyphs, which is a common size for font datasets. The algorithm was compared to other algorithms that use complex techniques to produce line connections, which require a significant amount of computational overhead and memory.

Following the approach of Gilmore and Schmitford, a single-order two-fluid model is developed to analyze the dynamics of Rayleigh-Bénard convection by considering the interactions between turbulent and cumulative fluid components, and the model is expanded to account for thermal diffusion at the interfaces between the two fluids. The resulting model leads to a scalar heat flux fluctuation equation that is analogous to the two-dimensional turbulent Taylor-Couette flow model proposed by Captain and Schmitford, and both models yield a $ \Delta T \propto \Delta T_{max}^{3/2} $ relationship. Numerical solutions to the two-fluid model's rescaled equations yield a $ Ra_{c} = 5.73 \times 10^9 $ critical Rayleigh number for the onset of chaotic convection, in close agreement with the $ 5.3 \times 10^9 $ value predicted by recent high-resolution numerical simulations. The model also provides a heat flux vs. temperature difference relationship that is consistent with existing experimental data. A key feature of the two-fluid model is its prediction that the heat flux will increase with an exponent of $ 1.5 $ when the temperature difference is below the maximum value, and will then approach a constant value as it approaches the maximum temperature difference. This is in line with the relationship predicted by the Captain and Schmitford model, and is supported by the results of numerical simulations. This research investigates how non-linear Yang-Mills charges impact the shadow radius and thermal profiles of black holes. We analyze thermodynamic properties of Yang-Mills-smeared black holes to determine the effects of non-linear Yang-Mills charges on their behavior. Our findings indicate that these charges contribute to an increased entropy, heat capacity, and critical pressure, all of which are essential in explaining the morphology of black hole shadows observed in the gravitational field of Yang-Mills fields. Additionally, we demonstrate that non-linear Yang-Mills charges lead to a larger shadow radius and distinct thermal profiles, depending on the spacetime dimensions and Yang-Mills non-linearity parameters. We also establish a relationship between the non-linear Yang-Mills charge and the radius of the shadow, ultimately suggesting that this radius serves as an indicator of the non-linear Yang-Mills charge strength. Furthermore, we establish that the non-linear Yang-Mills charge contributes to a first-order phase transition in the Yang-Mills-smeared Reissner-Nordström black holes. Lastly, we propose that the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter can be determined through astronomical observations of black hole shadows, providing a means to investigate the non-perturbative aspects of Yang-Mills theory in a gravitational context. This research is based on our previous work published in "Non-Linear Yang-Mills Charges and Black Hole Shadows" (arXiv: 2106.02383) and "Yang-Mills-Smeared Black Holes and the Non-Linear Yang-Mills Charge" (arXiv: 2106.02384).

Immersive video viewers like VR and AR headsets are becoming increasingly popular, but they pose a challenge by limiting the user's field of view. Reducing unnecessary video data enables faster loading times and minimizes processing power requirements. Accurate viewport prediction is essential for this optimization. Previous studies relied on additional data such as eye tracking or pupil detection, but these are costly and difficult to implement for large-scale applications. Instead, the text within the video, specifically subtitles, can be used to improve prediction accuracy without additional hardware. In this research, a subtitle-based viewport prediction model is developed that first identifies the spoken language to ensure the accuracy of text recognition, then uses a sequence-to-sequence model to forecast viewer attention based on the subtitles. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms baseline models by 21.1% in terms of mean squared error and 2.5% relative improvement in mean absolute error. The research also explores various factors that influence performance and provides a prototype that can be integrated into immersive video players available for download. The data and model associated with this work are accessible online.

Furthermore, we discuss potential applications and related problems for future research in this area.

Imitation learning enables robots to learn from demonstrations. Current algorithms rely on collecting numerous demonstrations, often requiring significant human effort, especially for complex tasks. This effort barrier can limit the learning process, as additional data is typically required for further improvement. In contrast, the TRAIL algorithm addresses this challenge by leveraging existing expert policies and making the most of limited demonstrations. TRAIL achieves this by employing an efficient learning routine that gradually refines the initial policy, using each new demonstration in a separate learning step to minimize waste. The result is a highly sample-efficient method that outperforms existing imitation learning algorithms, even when only a small number of demonstrations are provided. The TRAIL algorithm's performance is evaluated on the iCub dataset, which involves complex, human-provided demonstrations, and the results show that TRAIL performs better than current imitation learning algorithms, even with very few demonstrations. Recent studies combining reinforcement learning with neural machine translation have shown promising results. However, these approaches often rely on expensive exploration methods due to the large action space of replacing individual words with all possible words from a vocabulary. In our work, we address this challenge by reducing the action space to a smaller set of actions that are more relevant to the model's current state. Our experiments demonstrate that optimizing this compact action space leads to significant performance gains over traditional word-based action spaces. Moreover, we found that the optimal size of the action space varies depending on data quality, with smaller action spaces yielding greater performance benefits on smaller datasets. Our approach, which we call selective replacement, involves developing an activation function that maps the model's log-probabilities to a probability distribution over the action space. We also derive the gradient updates for this function, enabling efficient policy optimization. Our results indicate a notable improvement in performance, with performance gains of up to 1.6 BLEU points over the baseline model. Furthermore, we found that our approach leads to more interpretable models, with replacement distributions reflecting the model's understanding of the text, as validated through human evaluations. In our experiments, we achieved the best performance on three out of four machine translation tasks, outperforming the current state-of-the-art model by a margin of 1.4 BLEU points on the WMT2014 EN-DE dataset. Our work offers a novel perspective on the machine translation action space, presenting Selective Replacement as a versatile framework that can be applied to a broader range of sequence generation tasks and models. The code for our approach is openly available at https://github.com/zhengyf/Selective_Replacement.

In particular, we utilize a deep learning-based approach to leverage the combined data from the depth camera and a high-resolution RGB camera, resulting in a robust estimation framework that can handle various real-world scenarios. Recent studies utilizing Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs) have achieved notable success in image segmentation. This success can be attributed to the incorporation of edge information that aids in refining the prediction. However, the current approach of integrating edge information is limited to a basic multiplication operation between the edge gate and feature map components. This method fails to consider the distinct characteristics of the edge gate and feature map components. In response, this paper proposes an advanced Edge-Gated CNN (AEG-CNN) that incorporates an edge-gated module featuring parallel branches with additive and subtractive operations. The results of our experiments indicate that the proposed AEG-CNN yields enhanced performance in image segmentation when compared to the baseline model. Moreover, our method achieves a notable reduction in memory usage with minimal computational overhead. In particular, AEG-CNN exhibits a 4.85% improvement in mean accuracy and a 93.75% reduction in memory usage in the DUT-OMRON dataset. Furthermore, our method demonstrates a 3.41% improvement in mean accuracy and a 81.25% reduction in memory usage in the Baidu-OMRON dataset. The enhanced performance of AEG-CNN, combined with its optimized memory usage, makes it an appealing solution for edge-learned image segmentation tasks. The source code of our proposed AEG-CNN is openly accessible on the GitHub platform. Moreover, our model has been successfully deployed on the Baidu EdgeCloud platform. This deployment enables real-world applications of AEG-CNN in edge-learned image segmentation. Lastly, our research is accompanied by comprehensive evaluation protocols and experimental settings that provide a valuable reference for the development and assessment of new EG-CNN architectures. These protocols and settings are openly available on the Hugging Face Transformers platform. When machine learning models make mistakes during the prediction process, they often occur due to a lack of relevant past information. To mitigate this issue, we introduce the notion of hindsight summarization, which involves condensing prior knowledge into a more compact and informative form to supplement current information and enhance prediction accuracy. Building on this concept, we propose a neural summarization model that, through backward learning, refines its initial predictions based on subsequent outcomes and optimizes its summary representation to minimize attended prediction error. Evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate that our proposed model successfully reduces error rates in both classification and sequence tasks by leveraging prior knowledge from hidden layers, and we provide concrete examples highlighting the effectiveness of hindsight summarization. Furthermore, we explore various design aspects of the summarization model and the learning process, as well as the implications of our findings for the broader understanding of machine learning from a cognitive perspective. Current cross-cultural and multilingual emotion recognition systems face difficulties generalizing to new languages and datasets due to their inflexible structure. To address this limitation, we introduce the Feeling Transfer Network (FTN), a proposed framework that combines cross-cultural and multilingual capabilities using a dual modular design. This model consists of two key components: the Multilingual Emotion Feature Extractor (MEFE) and the Feeling Transfer Module (FTM). MEFE is a set of modular units that utilize multi-task learning to derive shared, language-specific emotion feature extractors for each language. These extractors are then combined with the help of FTM, allowing for the selection of the most suitable extractor to achieve optimal emotion recognition performance on a given dataset. To further enhance the model's performance and generalizability, we introduce the Feeling Transfer Module (FTM), a neural network that identifies the optimal extractor for each new dataset through a sample-efficient learning process. To support our proposal, we also established two multilingual emotion recognition datasets, MELD and MELD+, which comprise 26 Indian languages and 20 European languages, respectively. Experimental evaluations on these datasets demonstrate the superior performance of FTN over baseline models, particularly in scenarios involving few-shot learning. Additionally, an FTN-based system was successfully utilized in an user-centric emotion recognition application, showcasing the practical utility of this model. The source code and datasets are openly accessible at https://github.com/parth-agrawal/FTN. The code has been reviewed for validity according to the instructions provided.

Furthermore, we investigate the localized error bound comparison framework within the context of the value function, which represents the expected costs of future states, and determine that it follows a similar dynamic system to the original value function. The concept of intergenerational justice emphasizes the moral obligation to provide equal opportunities for all individuals to thrive, regardless of their birth circumstances. Intuitively, this principle suggests that those born later should have greater chances of achieving a higher standard of living. However, quantifying and measuring opportunities in this context is a complex task. In this paper, we introduce an innovative framework that views opportunities as assets that can be allocated among different generations, with the goal of maximizing the sum of logarithms of standards of living across time periods. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach by applying it to a simple dynamic general equilibrium model and show that fair intergenerational transfers can lead to significant improvements in welfare, especially benefiting later generations. These findings provide insights into the theoretical benefits of intergenerational justice and highlight the potential of our model to explore policy analyses and implications in real-world scenarios. Moreover, we discuss various methods for measuring opportunities and discuss the advantages and limitations of each approach. Furthermore, we discuss the significance of our framework in relation to existing research on intergenerational mobility, social mobility, and dynamic stochastic general equilibrium models. In addition, we discuss potential extensions to our model, including incorporating environmental aspects, international trade, and non-Log-Sum utility functions. Ultimately, our work offers a versatile tool for analyzing the dynamics of intergenerational mobility and transferring opportunities across generations. Additionally, we make our computational code publicly available to facilitate further research and enable policymakers to utilize our framework for policy-relevant simulations. In conclusion, our research offers a comprehensive approach to studying intergenerational mobility and transferring opportunities across generations, and we invite the academic community to build upon and contribute to this research. To better comprehend BART's performance, we introduce a new evaluation framework centered on partial tree linearization, a task that involves arranging words into a linear sequence based on their hierarchical relationship. We examine BART's capability in word ordering across multiple tasks and assess its effectiveness against human-annotated gold standards. Our analysis across three evaluation metrics-generate-from-samples, paraphrasing, and book chapter summarization-reveals BART to consistently struggle with word ordering, outperforming human standards only marginally. We also investigate the BART architecture's limitations in word ordering through a related task called partial tree linearization and discover that BART excels at this task when compared to other models, yet its results still fall short of human-annotated standards. We further examine the connection between word ordering and linearization barriers by classifying order-violating characters in words and finding a significant correlation with word ordering difficulties. We make our evaluation framework, data, and code publicly accessible to facilitate further analysis of BART's performance in word ordering. Moreover, we introduce the term order-aware evaluation to emphasize its significance. Additionally, we propose an order-aware variant of the BART model, where the order-aware variant outperforms the original BART model but still fails to meet human standards in word ordering. Recently, deepfake technology has emerged as a significant threat, particularly in the creation and dissemination of misleading visual information. Researchers have made notable progress in developing techniques to identify deepfakes, but their limitations mainly stem from solely utilizing either handcrafted features or single-source training data. To address these shortcomings, we propose DeepCraft, a novel multi-domain deepfake detection network that leverages cross-stitch connections to integrate both handcrafted and learned features, as well as fuse knowledge from multiple source domains. DeepCraft's architecture enables it to learn optimized aggregation pathways for both feature fusion and cross-domain adaptation. Empirical evaluations across three distinct datasets and utilizing three diverse source domains confirm that our framework achieves superior performance and enhanced adaptability in comparison to existing methods. Furthermore, our studies on the extracted features through multi-domain learning reveal that cross-stitch connections facilitate the incorporation of unique attributes from source domains, resulting in an enriched representation of handcrafted features that exhibits heightened discriminative power. Consequently, our work provides an enhanced multi-domain deepfake detection baseline, featuring an innovative approach to feature fusion and cross-domain adaptation that merits exploration in other related applications. The source code of our proposed framework is openly accessible on GitHub.

In the context of a weak decoy state QKD system that uses a vacuum and a single photon basis measurement, we identify an attack that allows an eavesdropper to bypass detection with a high probability, appearing as successful transmissions between the legitimate users. This attack flourishes in the weak decoy state QKD system's "key phase," which typically indicates optimal security, without being detected. As a result, an eavesdropper can gather sufficient entanglement units to compromise the system's security. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the proposed weak decoy state QKD system can be securely enhanced by converting it to a multi-photon basis measurement system. Simulation-based simulations and actual-world applications illustrate the advantages of this modification. As edge computing resources move closer to end-users, they consume less energy compared to transferring data to cloud servers. Optimizing energy efficiency at the edge can provide significant benefits, especially when combined with renewable energy sources. However, managing edge resources involves a complex problem due to conflicting objectives, such as balancing energy consumption and completion times. In this paper, we present an approximate algorithm based on the VND method with exchange and pathening strategies to minimize total energy consumption at the edge. Our results show that this method yields near-optimal solutions, and we also investigate various scenarios to analyze the energy efficiency of different scheduling policies. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of different optimization strategies on energy consumption, including a novel approach based on the VND method with local search, and we discuss the implications of our findings for future research in this area. Three candidate globular clusters, B6254, B6263, and B6267, located in the outer region of the Milky Way, have been studied using the Color-Magnitude Diagram (CMD). Initially identified through the Pan-STARRS1 survey, these objects were examined through a combination of ground-based optical imaging and the All-Sky Survey carried out by the Dark Energy Survey. The analysis of the CMD within a 1.5-$\sigma$ contour from the main-sequence turnoff point enabled the estimation of the clusters' metallicities and ages. The results revealed that B6254 and B6263 exhibit low metallicities, with the former estimated at 0.0004 ($-0.6$dex) and an age of 12.6 Gyr, while the latter showed a metal content of 0.0002 ($-0.8$dex) and an age of 11.3 Gyr. In contrast, B6267 displayed a higher metal content of 0.0014 ($-0.4$dex) along with an age of 10.3 Gyr. The location of these three clusters at large radii in the Milky Way highlights the richness of the outer halo and the significance of ongoing and future surveys in identifying and studying the most distant regions of the galaxy through the discovery of its oldest clusters. The age range of these three candidates, spanning from approximately 10 to 13 Gyr, is of particular interest as it bridges the gap between the most ancient globular clusters born during the galaxy's early formation and the younger population of the halo formed through the merger of smaller satellites during the galaxy's late stages of evolution. The discovery of B6254, B6263, and B6267 contributes to the growing list of outer-halo globular clusters with low metallic content and ancient ages, thereby supporting the multi-phase formation history of the galaxy. The chemical analysis of the cluster members in B6254 and B6263, conducted through the use of APOGEE spectra, has revealed an enhancement of $\alpha$-elements in B6254 and a decrease in the metallicity of B6263, providing further insight into the galaxy's evolution and the need for future studies of these and other newly discovered globular clusters in the outer regions of the Milky Way. In quantum information theory, erasure codes for specific types of tensors are used to mitigate the effects of information loss. These codes can be represented as tensor networks that adhere to particular constraints, effectively acting as channels that map parts of the input state to their erased counterparts. If a tensor network consists solely of a single type of tensor employed for erasure correction, it must follow certain rules based on the properties of that tensor. Furthermore, this tensor must comply with two fundamental conditions: it acts as a completely positive tensor, and all of its local marginal replicas share the same density. Based on these requirements, we derived an inequality rooted in quantum information theory, specifically an entanglement-assisted quantum erasure capacity theorem for multi-partite scenarios. This theorem provides the optimal rate for transmitting information about each party's quantum state, expressed as a fraction of the total entanglement-assisted quantum capacity, specifically the mixed-state version. This fraction is denoted as $E_{AA...}|_{EA}$. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a significant challenge in recent years due to the increasing availability of temporal and multi-relational data. Current time-encoding methods primarily focus on single-inference tasks, such as link prediction and classification, without consideration for the cyclic nature of temporal relations. This work introduces a novel cycle-aware time-encoding scheme for temporal relation paths of arbitrary length. The proposed encoding method leverages an attention-based mechanism and bidirectional recurrent neural networks to effectively capture the cyclic patterns and temporal dependencies within relations paths. The proposed attention-based time-encoding scheme also exhibits the ability to learn task-independent representations, with a strong correlation between the scores of the proposed prototype and existing studies on time-encoding schemes. Our results from a microscopic RPA theory match those from a macroscopic RPA model based on effective field theory. The RPA poles include multiple complex poles with distinct resonance characteristics, separating into three groups based on their resonance widths. The primary group, accounting for approximately 60$\%$ of the $B(E1)$ strength, is comprised of poles with relatively narrow width variations, ranging from 0.5 to 2.5 MeV. These findings support the applicability of a single-resonance RPA model to the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of a realistic nuclear force on the RPA poles, observing that their positions and widths are only moderately affected when using different nuclear forces. Building high-quality sentence representations from dense word embeddings like BERT is crucial in neural text-to-text tasks. Current methods that use dense-to-sparse transformations have shown promise but often lead to suboptimal results due to inefficient code generation algorithms and a lack of explicit sentence structure constraints. We present SparseGAN, a novel method that generates sentences in an efficient order, drawing upon the structural characteristics of dense input representations, including those from BERT. By combining a sentence generator with constraint layers that utilize input representations, we developed a sequential generator that leverages input representations to produce sentences that accurately reflect the underlying semantic structure. Furthermore, we found that the semantic structure of generated sentences closely mimics that of the underlying input representations, as demonstrated by a series of analyses, including those utilizing the WordSense Embedding Similarity Toolkit. Young star-forming regions and open clusters with minimal contamination from older stars are crucial for assessing the possibility of interstellar life dispersal, or panspermia. To identify the most promising candidates for this study, the authors analyzed infrared catalogues and optical star catalogues in four regions: Taurus, Ophiuchus, Upper Scorpius, and Beta Pic Moving Group. 

To isolate the most uncontaminated stellar samples, the authors applied the following criteria: 
1. The stars within each region should have similar distances to minimize bias.
2. The stellar sample should be dominated by young stars with low contamination from older stars.
3. The stars should be surrounded by a substantial molecular cloud, indicating a high likelihood of planetary systems.

Based on these criteria, the authors ranked the regions based on the proportion of young stars with low contamination from older stars. The Taurus region ranked highest, followed by Ophiuchus and Upper Scorpius, with the Beta Pic Moving Group showing the highest contamination rate due to its age and distance from the Sun. 

To estimate the potential for life dispersal through panspermia, the authors calculated the number of stars that could travel between the stellar groups without encountering significant obstacles, such as massive stars and supernovae, and being ejected from the galactic plane. The authors found that the Taurus region and Ophiuchus have a high potential for panspermia, while Upper Scorpius and the Beta Pic Moving Group have lower potential due to their age and location.

The problem of identifying the minimum power required to establish edge disjoint paths in a network has significant implications for the reliability and performance of data transmission. Building upon previous research, we investigate the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, which involves determining the minimum power needed to connect nodes s and t, while also finding the fewest edge disjoint paths between them. We examine the computational complexity of this problem and its variants, as well as the relationships between them. Furthermore, we analyze the complexity of generating the fewest edge disjoint st-Paths, and we present an algorithm for calculating the minimum power required for k edge disjoint st-Paths when the power levels of the network's edges are restricted to two possible values. We also explore the connection between Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths and the Minimum Power k Edge Disjoint Paths problem, which involves identifying the minimum power needed for edge disjoint paths between all pairs of nodes. This research provides a foundation for addressing critical issues in wireless communication systems, and we expect it to contribute to ongoing work related to network design and performance optimization. 

Keywords: Minimum Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths, Minimum Power k Edge Disjoint Paths, Computational Complexity, Network Design, Performance Optimization.

Enhancing optical character recognition (OCR) systems for document images that incorporate external knowledge, particularly those containing forms, is a complex challenge. One significant obstacle in this process is accurately linking the pre-printed text from these documents to relevant pieces of user-generated text, including emails. This task is further complicated by the presence of noisy document images. In our research, a novel end-to-end approach called Email Form Reader is proposed to bridge this gap. It involves using a deep learning technique called attention-augmented optical character recognition (AA-OCR) to improve the accuracy of OCR systems when processing document images. Additionally, a separate neural network called attention-augmented text classifier (AA-TC) is employed to classify documents into specific email categories based on the extracted text. The classification process is performed independently of the email content and only relies on the text classification features that are learned during the training phase. In our experiments, the proposed Email Form Reader system demonstrated significant enhancements over existing methods, achieving a 36% increase in overall accuracy and a 12% boost in form-field accuracy when dealing with noisy document images. Furthermore, our research showcased the ability of AA-OCR to accurately detect relationships between pre-printed text and input text with a 63% increase in F1-score. The Email Form Reader system also exhibited improved performance in real-world applications, achieving a 25% increase in overall accuracy and a 15% improvement in form-field accuracy when processing real document images. In our research, we introduced a new dataset called Email Forms Dataset, which consists of 15,000 document-image-to-text pairs spanning 100 different email categories. Our research was made possible through collaborations with data annotators and email account holders who contributed over 10,000 annotated document images and corresponding email content in exchange for incentives. In our experiments, the proposed Email Form Reader system was compared to traditional OCR systems and learning-based approaches, resulting in significant improvements in accuracy. The proposed AA-OCR and AA-TC models were found to outperform these alternatives by a substantial margin, achieving a 30% increase in overall accuracy and a 10% boost in form-field accuracy when dealing with noisy document images. In our research, we explored various techniques to improve the performance of the Email Form Reader system, including utilizing pre-trained models, incorporating external knowledge, and employing attention-augmented networks. Our research has far-reaching implications for the development of document-image-to-text systems, particularly those containing forms, and has made the proposed Email Forms Dataset available for public use. Euler-Maruyama is demonstrated to be a simple yet effective sampling method for post-learning analysis of HiP-RSSMs, enabling the generation of realistic data sets, evaluation of forecasting performance, and visualization of latent state dynamics. The benefits of these techniques are showcased through a dynamic system case study involving the generation of synthetic music. This research provides an accessible framework for using HiP-RSSMs in the analysis and simulation of stochastic processes. All code used in this research is available online. Developers utilizing functional programming often encounter difficulties when debugging their code due to the absence of side effects. In Functional Java, a popular and widely taught variant of the language, debugging is complicated by the lack of explicit statements directing the control flow and the use of higher-order functions that envelop variables in their own scope. Our research focuses on enhancing the educational value of assignments and assessments by streamlining the debugging process for students. It integrates an automated testing tool with a presentation layer that provides a simplified interface for identifying and addressing errors, thereby increasing student understanding and minimizing the time spent on grading. This system was initially developed for CTU's "Introduction to Functional Programming" course, utilizing Scala and Play Framework for Web development, and it has been successfully employed to evaluate the effectiveness of the system through both qualitative and statistical assessments. One promising approach to enhance model performance with minimal labeled data is the Iterative Logits Ensemble (ILE) method. ILE starts by employing an ensemble of models to produce initial predictions on a small labeled subset of data. It then iteratively incorporates the remaining vast amount of unlabeled data with the following steps until convergence: utilizing the ensemble to produce a new set of logits for data points, training a new model using the logits from the ensemble, and training another model using the logits from the new ensemble. The Pairwise ILE (PILE) is an improved version of ILE, where the ensemble and model training process occurs on a pairwise level instead of the entire dataset. It has also been mathematically shown that PILE converges faster than ILE. Moreover, PILE can be viewed as utilizing label information through an ensemble-based pseudo-loss function. The closed-form solution of PILE makes it more efficient than the iterative ILE method. Quantum annealing is an optimization technique derived from quantum mechanics that has generated significant interest for solving complex computational problems. This process involves gradually modifying a system from a known state to solve an unknown problem. Researchers have expressed concerns that environmental interference (decoherence) could impede the effectiveness of quantum annealing. To investigate this, a joint quantum-classical framework was developed to analyze the interplay between decoherence and quantum annealing. Using this framework, a general condition was identified to prevent successful outcome production in quantum annealing. Furthermore, the model was applied to examine the influence of different environmental interactions on quantum annealing in both idealized and realistic scenarios. The findings suggest that decoherence can hinder the achievement of the target ground state, especially when quantum annealing is ineffectively designed. Conversely, well-designed quantum annealing is more resilient to environmental interference. To further enhance performance, the most beneficial classical pre-optimization strategies were determined based on environmental characteristics. The results indicate that decoherence can be managed through a combination of classical pre-optimization and quantum control, ultimately holding promise for the practical applications of quantum annealing.

Deep neural network architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent Neural Networks, are often characterized by numerous parameters that require a large dataset for training. This research introduces local critic training, a technique that utilizes smaller subsets of data to train a network from a coarsely initialized starting point. The goal of the coarse training stage isn't to achieve optimal performance but rather to generate a network that can serve as a starting point for refined training on the full dataset. The benefits of local critic training are showcased through its application to Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent Neural Networks, demonstrating enhanced training efficiency with no compromise on accuracy. Furthermore, we find that local critic training offers resistance to data poisoning attacks, making it an attractive method for developing robust deep neural networks with minimal additional data. We also explore the theoretical implications of local critic training and its connection to generalizing the technique to other optimization algorithms. The source code for our method is openly available at https://github.com/chen308/Local-Critic-Optimization. 

Keywords: Deep Neural Networks, Efficient Training, Robust Learning, Data Subsets, Contrastive Learning, Optimization Algorithms.
