Distributions defined through their cumulative distribution functions at unspecified points raise significant computational hurdles, necessitating the development of specialized estimation methods. This study presents a novel, general framework for approximating entropies and other information quantities that can be applied to a broad range of distribution types, including those represented by their cumulative distribution functions at unspecified points. The proposed framework is versatile and adaptable to different computational requirements, enabling the use of different order statistics-based estimation methods to balance precision and computational efficiency. The framework's efficacy is demonstrated through the example of two well-known distribution families - the Pareto and the exponential - for which the standard cumulative distribution function does not provide sufficient information to compute quantities like Shannon entropy directly. Consequently, new estimation methods are derived and evaluated within this context. The findings are subsequently applied to the situation where a cumulative distribution function is available at specified points, a scenario common to real-world data sets. The proposed framework is made available as an open-source Python package called estimators-info on GitHub, accompanied by a comprehensive example using the scikit-entropy library. The derived methods are further assessed in terms of precision across a diverse range of standard continuous distributions, including those for which the cumulative distribution function is available at unspecified points. The study also explores the impact of diverse computational strategies on the precision of approximations, including the use of different order statistics, Monte Carlo estimation, and the application of different statistical tests. The findings are expected to contribute to a better understanding of the properties and estimation challenges of information quantities in complex, real-world scenarios. The derived methods are intended to facilitate further research in this area and make the proposed framework's results verifiable and reproducible. Dynamic graph classification is a complex task due to the varying structure of graphs over time, which requires a high degree of flexibility in the representation of temporal graph data. Most current approaches, which primarily utilize time-series extensions of graph kernels or initial embedding techniques, have significant limitations in capturing the temporal evolution of graphs. To address this issue, we propose DECENNT, a novel dynamic graph classification framework that utilizes neural tangent kernels to generate representations of temporal graph data. DECENNT consists of multiple NTK encoders that process individual graph snapshots, producing representation vectors for each encoder. These vectors are then combined through an attention mechanism to obtain a unified representation for the entire temporal graph. Furthermore, DECENNT enables flexible modeling of temporal evolution through a fixed number of intermediate representations. Experimental results on multiple classification tasks reveal that DECENNT achieves superior performance compared to existing graph kernel and embedding-based methods. Moreover, an in-depth analysis of model components and hyperparameters provides valuable insights into optimizing the classification accuracy of DECENNT. The code and data for DECENNT are openly accessible at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/decennet.

The study of stochastic processes is crucial for reconstructing phylogenies and understanding evolutionary dynamics. In nature, various processes such as gene flow, selection, migration, recombination, and genetic drift generate complex patterns that evolve over time, affecting the structure and function of biological systems. To tackle these challenges, researchers employ mathematical models that describe the behavior of systems under specific processes, often represented as Markov diffusion processes. In this review, we explore recent developments in identifying the underlying Markov diffusion processes responsible for observed empirical patterns, particularly in genomics. This endeavor is an inverse problem that requires estimating a system's past based on its current state, using dynamic equations that describe the system's behavior over time. We discuss cutting-edge methods that leverage empirical patterns, statistical tools, and computational algorithms to approximate the underlying processes. These methods include Bayesian approaches, score-based models, hidden Markov models, and deep learning techniques. We also examine the application of these methods to various biological systems and processes, including the evolution of genomes, gene families, and amino acid and nucleotide sequences. While these studies have made significant progress, there are numerous challenges to be addressed, such as the limited size of empirical data samples, the complexity of systems, and the scarcity of theoretical guarantees for some algorithms. To overcome these obstacles, future research should prioritize the development of more efficient algorithms, utilize multiple data sources, and explore new statistical approaches. Ultimately, solving the inverse problem of Markov diffusion processes will provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms driving evolutionary systems and shed light on the complex evolutionary processes that have shaped life on Earth. Futhermore, the analytical techniques developed for this problem will have a broader impact on the study of other complex systems and processes. 

This review is an extension of a previous article published in 2020, which focused on forward models describing Markov diffusion processes and their applications in evolutionary biology. In contrast, this update is centered on the inverse problem of identifying the underlying processes responsible for observed empirical patterns, which has become a critical area of research in the field.

Transforming complex waves into their component forms is crucial for understanding and manipulating light-matter interactions. This concept is particularly relevant for enhancing scattering, absorption, and fluorescence in nanostructures. To achieve this, it's essential to identify the orthogonal eigenchannels and corresponding intensity patterns in the transmission matrix of a sample. Our research provides a statistical framework for determining eigenchannels and associated intensity profiles in partially broken and randomly fragmented situations. We demonstrate that even in such cases, the main eigenchannels still maintain a direct relationship with the original intensity patterns, albeit with some deviation, and can be used to reconstruct the original wave front. This alignment is confirmed through numerical simulations and experimental validation using digital holography. Our study offers a practical approach to extracting relevant information about a complex wave using a distorted version of the transmission matrix. This information can be applied to improve optical scattering, absorption, and fluorescence in nanostructures and other areas.

In a scenario where a natural solution to the hierarchy problem exists beyond the Standard Model, there is a significant likelihood of discovering multiple Higgs bosons in the near future. To thoroughly assess the theoretical implications of such discoveries, it is essential to thoroughly investigate the production processes of these heavy Higgs bosons at next-to-leading order in QCD, taking into consideration the impact of squarks. In this research, we have computed the QCD NLO corrections to gluon-induced heavy Higgs boson production in a general effective field theory framework, accounting for the influence of light quark and heavy quark contributions. We have developed publicly accessible numerical code to automate these calculations for a broad category of heavy Higgs bosons, including the CP-even scalar $a$ and the pseudoscalar $A$, the charged Higgs boson $H^{\pm}$, and the CP-odd scalar $H$. Furthermore, we have examined the squark contributions to these processes, demonstrating how the phases of the relevant parameters affect the theoretical predictions. In collaboration with the LHC, we have provided detailed numerical results for the production of a heavy Higgs boson in gluon fusion and vector boson fusion at 14 and 13 TeV, as well as in associated production with a bottom quark or top quark at 14 and 7 TeV, respectively. In these scenarios, we have incorporated theoretical uncertainties associated with missing higher-order contributions, employing the NNLLA resummation of soft gluon contributions to enhance the precision of our predictions. In the case of gluon-induced production, we have also incorporated the impact of squarks, presenting results for various squark masses. In the context of effective field theory, we have compared our results to existing studies, in particular those based on the effective potential approach. In the case of heavy Higgs boson production in the context of the minimal supersymmetric Standard Model, we have provided detailed numerical results for the production of a heavy Higgs boson in gluon fusion and vector boson fusion at 14 and 13 TeV, as well as in associated production with a bottom quark or top quark at 14 and 7 TeV, respectively. This paper introduces a new high-frequency test for complex systems with non-identifiable parameters by drawing on the concepts of network autoregressive models and Gaussian graphical models. The proposed test bypasses the difficulties of identifying parameters in high-frequency data by utilizing a network-based approach, which enables us to develop a test even in cases with no identifiable parameters. We demonstrate the theoretical properties of this test, showing that it achieves the desired asymptotic distribution required for a valid test, even in the presence of non-identifiable parameters. We also provide a practical implementation of the test, along with a numerical example to illustrate its application. Furthermore, we conduct a simulation study to evaluate the performance of the test in various scenarios, including different network topologies, degrees of non-identifiability, and sample sizes. The results of these simulations are consistent with our theoretical findings and confirm the test's efficacy in a range of scenarios. The paper also includes an empirical analysis of financial market data, examining the relationships between stock returns and volatility in the S&P 500 index and finding evidence of spillover effects. The code and data used in this study are available online. Finally, we outline potential future research directions, which may involve extending the test to accommodate other types of networks and relaxing the assumptions required for its application. Keywords: network autoregressive models, high-frequency data, non-identifiable parameters, spillover effects.

The efficiency of solving dynamic optimization models is often hampered by the high computational cost of the backward pass, which can be mitigated by leveraging problem structure. This study introduces an innovative dual decomposition approach for solving DAE models that utilize function structures to achieve significant performance enhancements. By utilizing function structures, our approach can: (1) utilize sparse matrix operations for the backward pass; (2) employ an iterative technique to solve for residual vectors; (3) leverage asynchronous computation to utilize multiple CPU cores. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach through a dynamic energy model, which showcases a substantial reduction in backward pass computation time and overall solution time with the use of multiple cores. Furthermore, our approach enables us to solve larger-scale dynamic optimization problems with over 65,000 decision variables. By incorporating our approach into the GAMS framework via the SNOPT solver, our research offers a practical solution for solving large DAE optimization problems with nonlinear models and nonconvex objectives or constraints. This research builds upon our previous work on function structures, sparse matrix operations, and asynchronous forward solving, and provides a valuable solution for efficiently solving large DAE optimization problems. However, it is essential to note that our approach may not be as computationally efficient as specialized dynamic optimization solvers, particularly those that leverage highly customized solvers and/or graphical processing units (GPUs) for computation. Nonetheless, our approach offers a valuable solution for problems solved via GAMS, particularly those with large dynamic optimization components. This research is relevant to any field of study that employs dynamic optimization models, especially those with complex, nonlinear structures. Examples of such fields include energy economics, environmental management, and engineering design. In these fields, dynamic optimization models are frequently employed to analyze long-term problems, and solving these models efficiently is crucial for maintaining computational performance as models scale up. In our research, we demonstrate the benefits of our approach through a dynamic energy model, which is a critical component of many energy and environmental models. To comprehend cell mechanics, it's essential to study individual stress fibers within cells. Our experiments utilizing a force-clamp microscope revealed that the mechanical properties of single stress fibers are influenced by contractility, which we found to be a key property governing their behavior. We developed an advanced finite element model that accounted for contractility and cellular ultrastructure to simulate stress fiber mechanics and force transmission to the cell membrane. By applying this model to cultured fibroblast cells, we mapped contractility along stress fibers and across the cell cortex, which we found to be concentrated at stress fiber nodes and within 1 micron of the cell edge. This concentration of contractility near the cell edge is what drives force transmission to adhesions sites, which are located just 0.5 to 1.5 microns from the cell edge. We also discovered that contractility is higher along polarized stress fibers and that cellular asymmetry is caused by localized increases in contractility along the stress fibers on the heavier side. Stress fiber contraction is accelerated by adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and slowed by adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which is consistent with previous research. Finally, we demonstrated that contractility is a critical factor in stress fiber mechanics and cell mechanics, especially in regions with high contractility, which we found to be similar to areas identified by microrheology. By studying contractility and stress fiber mechanics, we can now better understand how cells reorganize their actin cytoskeleton in response to changes in adhesion sites and culture conditions. In contrast, this study examines the cyclic characteristics of these graphs over time to better understand cryptocurrency-based crimes. An advanced detection method for negative cycles was developed and evaluated using real-world data from the Ethereum cryptocurrency network. The results showed a significant connection between negative cycles and malicious transactions and revealed that the detection method's effectiveness depends greatly on the time frame considered. With a focus on a time frame of 10-20 days, the study established upper and lower limits for the accuracy and precision of the detection method. The findings also indicated that the method's performance could be fine-tuned to identify specific types of negative cycles associated with malicious transactions. To facilitate further research, the study introduced an open-source tool for detecting negative cycles within temporal transaction graphs. The results of the study can serve as a foundation for future research aimed at enhancing the detection of cryptocurrency-based crimes. Cloud-based HPC systems face significant obstacles in achieving low latency and high bandwidth due to the latency inherent in accessing remote memory and the limited bandwidth of network connections. Memory-intensive HPC workloads, such as those resulting from simulations, are particularly hindered by these constraints, making them less suitable for cloud-based execution. To mitigate this, a technique called Remote Queue Optimization is proposed to enhance the efficiency of memory access operations by prioritizing local memory usage and minimizing the reliance on distant memory. This approach involves a system model that separates memory requests into distinct categories based on their origin, with a resulting system that exhibits up to 2 times improvement in throughput and up to 2 times reduction in average job completion time. Furthermore, simulations indicate that a system employing RQO can achieve comparable performance to that of a specialized HPC system, even when memory access latency is as high as 1000 times network latency. RQO has been implemented on Amazon Web Services and OpenStack cloud platforms, with observed gains in performance. To facilitate the adoption of RQO, an open-source framework called CloudQueue is being made available to facilitate seamless integration with cloud providers and HPC applications. This framework is now being offered to the broader research community in the form of an open-source codebase. As a result of these advancements, memory-intensive HPC applications can now run on cloud-based systems with improved efficiency, enabling on-demand access to supercomputing capabilities and paving the way for further innovation in cloud HPC even in the presence of high memory access latency. In the linear contextual bandit problem, an agent navigates through a context-space that is divided into distinct regions, each representing a particular context distribution. The agent selects actions in response to observed context variables, aiming to balance exploration with exploitation to maximize an unknown reward function that is linked to a set of actionable features. To make decisions efficiently, the agent needs an estimate of the context distribution's parameters and the reward function, which can be acquired through data collection. To facilitate data sharing, the agent communicates a compact summary of its context distribution to a central controller, which allocates resources to the agent based on this summary. In many applications, including recommendation systems and advertising, the context distribution's structure aligns with a probability model that is discrete and tractable. To tackle this problem, an efficient contextual linear bandit algorithm is proposed, which generates a summary of the context distribution's parameters to aid a discrete resource allocation decision. The algorithm's performance is analyzed under various assumptions about the context distribution, and a worst-case bit count is derived for communication, which scales logarithmically with the number of actions. To address scenarios where the context distribution's structure is unknown, an alternative approach is proposed, which involves estimating the context distribution directly, resulting in a bit count that scales linearly with the dimension of the context space. The proposed algorithms are evaluated in simulations and real-world online advertising datasets. The code for the context distribution estimation method is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/ContextLinearBandit. The research is relevant to various applications involving discrete context distributions, including recommendation systems, advertising, and signal processing systems. While Agile methodologies like Scrum have proven effective for in-person teams, there's a noticeable gap in literature regarding their effectiveness in a fully remote setting. Our research aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining how team members working from home utilize Scrum practices and identify factors influencing project success in a remote environment. We've developed and empirically tested a theory-based framework using both quantitative and qualitative methods. A survey of 137 remote software development teams provided statistical analysis, supplemented by in-depth case studies of four teams to gain a deeper understanding of Scrum implementation and project dynamics. Our findings indicate significant associations between team adaptability, trust, and performance metrics such as meeting deadlines and project quality. Notably, we found that some teams successfully incorporated essential Scrum practices despite remote work challenges. Our research offers a framework and set of testable hypotheses for further study in various remote work contexts. By acknowledging the potential for teams to thrive in a fully virtual setting, we challenge existing assumptions about the need for face-to-face interaction in Agile methodologies. Our work contributes to a broader discussion on the effectiveness of Agile methodologies in a post-pandemic world and beyond. It is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.04951. In policy learning, using approximate value functions that are efficiently calculated has become a popular approach. Despite initial successes, previous fast value function estimates were found to be inaccurate when applied to diverse testing datasets. This research reveals that the performance of fast value function estimates is heavily influenced by the size of the testing dataset and the size of the training dataset. Specifically, when the training dataset is large in comparison to the testing dataset, an efficient value function estimate that requires minimal computations is typically preferred. However, when the testing dataset is substantial in comparison to the training dataset, more complex efficient value function estimates tend to outperform their simpler counterparts. This research also introduces an initial framework for selecting the best fast value function estimate based on the relative sizes of the training and testing datasets. The proposed framework leads to enhanced policy performance, ultimately yielding a data-driven approach that chooses the most effective efficient value function estimate. This choice is determined by the ratio of the training and testing dataset sizes, and has been found to yield better results than previous approaches that relied on fixed or adaptive thresholds. The data-driven approach has been evaluated on multiple datasets and scenarios, yielding superior results compared to both the baseline policy and a previously established state-of-the-art method. The code for this research is openly accessible on the Meta World repository. Additionally, the paper includes an analysis of the benefits of efficient value function learning, particularly in scenarios with limited data, and has been made openly accessible on arXiv. Further research aims to expand this work to other domains and value function types. Ultimately, this research is a significant step towards accelerating policy evaluation and the utilization of approximate value functions in reinforcement learning tasks. Moreover, the findings of this research have been confirmed through multiple evaluations, and the data and models are openly accessible for replication and further study. We investigated the binary power control scheme in large, complex wireless networks, comparing its effectiveness to optimal power control. Through numerical analysis and case studies based on real-world applications, we found that the binary scheme, despite its simplicity, achieves nearly the same performance as optimal power control, with only a minor decrease in throughput. This minimal loss is offset by the significant gain of easier implementation and reduced computational complexity. Our findings suggest that complex algorithms are not always necessary to achieve good results in this context. We also confirmed that the near-equality in performance between binary and optimal power control holds not just in our custom-generated networks, but also in real-world scenarios, specifically in cellular networks and ad-hoc networks with high interference levels. A key factor in this performance equality is the large size of our tested networks, as smaller networks reveal a more substantial gap between binary and optimal power control performance. In such smaller networks, however, a more advanced scheme achieves comparable results to binary power control, further highlighting the complex interplay between network size, interference levels, and computational complexity in evaluating the efficacy of power control methods. We also observed that the near-equality in performance between binary and optimal power control is reached when the average number of active transceivers in a given node's vicinity is at least around 10 times the number of degrees in that node's local network. This finding has implications for the design of power control algorithms, particularly in large and complex networks. We conclude that in such environments, binary power control is a viable and efficient solution, outperforming optimal power control in terms of computational complexity while incurring only a minor loss in throughput. This result is significant, especially considering the potential for future networks to rival the scale and complexity of current systems. As future work, we suggest investigating whether our findings can be applied to a broader range of network types and topologies. Additionally, the potential benefits of the binary scheme's simplicity for distributed power control implementations and the scheme's robustness in the presence of failures and dynamic network changes are also areas worthy of exploration. Finally, while our simulations utilized a general, purpose-built network architecture, future research could also benefit from using real, custom-designed networks as input parameters. To enhance the computational efficiency of complex flow simulations involving numerous time steps, we present a novel multiple-time-step integration algorithm that integrates separate time steps for the flow field and particle interactions. By leveraging an intermediate time step, the proposed method allows for a significant increase in the time step size while maintaining similar accuracy to traditional methods. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach through numerical tests of a simple example and three scenarios of multi-body problems, demonstrating its ability to boost computational performance while upholding the same level of precision. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of distinct time steps on the algorithm's performance and offer suggestions for optimizing its efficiency. Additionally, we examine the method's applicability to two different solver types: a built-in explicit Navier-Stokes solver and an external implicit solver. We observed a notable increase in computational speed, with the most efficient solution being achieved with an eightfold increase in time step size, resulting in a corresponding decrease in total simulation time. However, this was contingent upon the specific problem being solved, the chosen solver type, and the resulting particle motion relative to the flow field. We also validated our method against a direct numerical simulation of a long-term Navier-Stokes equation solution, with the added presence of particles, utilizing the proposed algorithm to solve the combined problem. The results showed that our method yielded an accurate solution for both the flow field and particles, with negligible errors, thus confirming its effectiveness. We believe our multiple-time-step algorithm offers an efficient and reliable solution for accelerating the computation of complex flow simulations involving multiple time steps. It has the potential to streamline the numerical solution of these intricate problems, making it more feasible to tackle even more demanding scenarios in the future. This paper introduces a feedback control system for a robotic hopping mechanism that moves across soft terrain. The robot's dynamic movement is represented by a continuous-time nonlinear model, and the control algorithm is based on a discrete-time feedback model. By applying the feedback control, the algorithm successfully tracks a target trajectory in real-time during both the robot's hop phase and its descent and takeoff phases. The algorithm's effectiveness was verified through simulations using the MATLAB software. Furthermore, an experimental setup was constructed using a soft terrain platform and a DSPACE hardware-in-loop system to test the algorithm on actual robotic hops. The results showed that the feedback control system is capable of accurately tracking a target trajectory over soft terrain. Additionally, the algorithm was found to be robust in controlling the robot's movement during both the hop phase and the descent and takeoff phases. The proposed feedback control system has the potential to contribute to the development of robotic applications that involve hopping on soft terrain. The algorithm's ability to operate in real-time makes it suitable for use in conjunction with vision-based target tracking systems. The method's robustness could also enable the robotic hopping mechanism to navigate complex, soft environments that require adaptive movement. This research investigates the impact of significant oscillations in a droplet on the transfer of heat and mass in the surrounding gas. A key aspect studied is the effect of droplet deformation on convective heat transfer and the associated changes in temperature and concentration distributions. Numerical simulations utilizing a level-set method and solver for the Navier-Stokes equations accurately capture the droplet's movements, breakdown into multiple droplets, and resulting enhanced mass transfer enhancement due to increased surface area. Initially stable droplets undergo large amplitude oscillations when subject to intense acoustic fields, but ultimately break apart into smaller droplets that transfer mass more efficiently. The findings show a notable increase in convective heat transfer caused by the droplet's irregular shape, and reveal that increased mass transfer is primarily attributed to enhanced convective transfer rather than diffusion. Furthermore, the effect of a surrounding gas flow on droplets was also examined, revealing that even in low acoustic pressure conditions, the droplet's shape and size can change sufficiently to impact mass and heat transfer. This research has implications for understanding the behavior of droplets in complex, real-world environments.

The primary objective of negation, a critical component in human language, is to convey disagreement or refusal. Despite its simplicity, identifying and classifying negation in automated systems has proven exceptionally challenging. In this research, we examine negation in medical texts to determine its impact on natural language understanding and classification tasks. Our extensive analysis of negation reveals significant disparities between human and machine performance, with machine learning models struggling to match human levels of accuracy even when trained on extensive datasets. Our findings indicate that negation poses a unique challenge for natural language processing models, leading to inaccuracies in both syntax and semantics. To better comprehend the complex relationships between language and meaning, we advocate for a more nuanced approach to language understanding that takes into account the intricate aspects of language. In the context of our experiments, we demonstrate that models overreliance on data leads to a neglect of negation, resulting in decreased performance on classification tasks. To mitigate this effect, we propose augmenting models with negation markers, yielding a notable improvement in performance. Ultimately, our research underscores the significance of negation in determining the quality of natural language understanding and highlights the value of incorporating semantic aspects of language in classification tasks. The datasets and models utilized in this research are freely accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek19/Negation-Analysis for the benefit of the broader NLP community. Futhermore, we release the NLP-Fellows dataset used in this research at https://github.com/Abhishek19/NLP-Fellows. Additionally, we introduce the NLP-Fellows evaluation framework, a collection of tasks designed to assess the capabilities of NLP models in a more realistic setting, mirroring human performance on complex tasks. This framework is available at https://github.com/Abhishek19/NLP-Fellows. In the context of our research, the NLP-Fellows framework comprises 13 tasks, including the negation classification and semantic reasoning tasks examined in this research, in addition to 5 other tasks. Determining the annealing gap requires solving the invariant equation, which describes the steady-state of the Hamiltonian at different points during the quantum annealing process. In this research, an in-depth analysis of the annealing gap is performed by classifying the equilibrium states of the Hamiltonian under quantum annealing, resulting in the derivation of an invariant equation that can be applied to any quantum annealing protocol. The study specifically examines the Kadowaki-Tabuchi protocol and investigates the relationship between the number of qubits and the annealing gap. The findings indicate that the gap increases exponentially with the number of qubits, specifically 4.58 times its base value for each additional qubit. The research also presents a numerical method for solving the invariant equation, which enables the direct computation of the annealing gap. The study suggests that understanding the annealing gap is crucial for optimizing quantum annealing protocols, and it is shown that the gap can be minimized through the application of resonant quantum annealing. The traditional alignment techniques used in process execution analysis, such as infix and postfix alignments, compare the structures of two processes by matching corresponding operator values in a first-in-first-out (FIFO) order. However, real-world processes often follow a last-in-first-out (LIFO) order, prompting the need for a new analysis method. To address this, we propose a method to analyze LIFO processes by utilizing a stack-based system. Additionally, we have developed a notation to represent the structure of processes using infix and postfix notations, which can be translated into each other. This paper introduces a novel approach called SVD-based software variation management (SVM). SVM leverages the properties of singular value decomposition (SVD) to effectively track and represent the evolving nature of software systems. By applying SVD to matrices constructed from their source code, SVM can identify and quantify the differences between variations of a software system, enabling efficient organization and management of its evolving components. Furthermore, SVM facilitates the discovery of latent software variations by pinpointing nonzero singular values in the SVD output, thereby enhancing the performance of search algorithms used for variant detection. Our method was evaluated using the Zephyr operating system as well as a set of Linux kernel variants, demonstrating its capability to accurately model and manage complex software evolutions. In comparison to existing methods, our results show that SVM excels at locating new software variations, achieving a precision rate of 80% which surpasses the 50% precision achieved by alternative methods in the same experiment conditions. The techniques presented in this paper can be applied to other software systems that exhibit similar structure and evolution dynamics. The implementation of our method is available as an open-source project on GitHub, consisting of approximately 5000 lines of Python code utilizing popular libraries such as NumPy, SciPy, and matplotlib for its visualization tools. As for future directions, we suggest exploring ways to integrate SVD-based software variation management with existing maintenance and development workflows, along with investigating other dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA to compare their effectiveness against SVD. In the face of public health emergencies like the COVID-19 pandemic, social media has become a primary source of information for both the general public and healthcare professionals. Twitter, in particular, has emerged as a crucial platform for disseminating vital information, opinions, and sentiments that can significantly influence people's behavior and decision-making processes. Consequently, accurately capturing the emotional tone of Twitter data during such crises has become increasingly important for developing effective predictive models in healthcare. However, doing so efficiently becomes computationally expensive when dealing with large volumes of Twitter data due to Twitter's restrictive API policies, which enforce a maximum of 5000 distinct IDs per request. To address this challenge, we present a novel, efficient, and scalable approach called Multi-Batch Sentiment Analysis (MBSA) that leverages multiple parallel workers to process separate, randomly selected subsets of data simultaneously. We have experimentally validated the MBSA approach on large-scale Twitter datasets from the COVID-19 pandemic era, demonstrating that it not only achieves superior performance compared to traditional single-batch methods but also significantly reduces training time by up to 50% with minimal compromise on accuracy. Furthermore, our research reveals that employing an intermediate layer with a reduced number of hidden units can lead to further performance enhancements. The MBSA approach has been successfully applied to two critical applications: predicting public sentiment towards recommended COVID-19 vaccination strategies and identifying influential Twitter users based on their sentiment. Our findings have been made publicly available through our research repository. We have also released the MBSA code as an open-source contribution to the deep learning community.

Through numerical simulations of a 0.5 solar mass T Tauri star T Tauri system, our research reveals that dust cooling is severely restricted in the inner disk due to high temperatures and the associated photodissociation of molecules, making dust ineffective at this stage. Machine learning models are increasingly being utilized in high-stakes applications where their reliability cannot be compromised. Research into backdoor attacks, which enable a malicious model to secretly classify data in favor of the attacker, holds significant implications for the trustworthiness of these models. However, most existing studies on backdoor attacks are limited to single-task scenarios, which do not reflect the real-world scenario where multiple tasks are often intertwined. In this research, we address this limitation by developing a dynamic backdoor attack that targets multiple OOD tasks. The attack involves introducing a time-varying trigger feature and a corresponding activation function for each target task, which presents several challenges due to the limited labeled data available. We propose an activation function with a compact representation that can be learned efficiently using an activation encoder, which enables the efficient transfer of the activation function to OOD target tasks. Furthermore, we introduce a trigger feature generator that can generate trigger features for OOD target tasks with high accuracy using a generator discriminator, which allows the efficient incorporation of new target tasks without retraining the model. Experimental results on multiple OOD tasks, including both low-dimensional and high-dimensional data, demonstrate the effectiveness of our dynamic backdoor attack. Moreover, an activation encoder and generator discriminator that can be trained with just a few labeled samples show that our method can be applied to real-world scenarios. Additionally, we found that the activation function plays a critical role in determining the difficulty of the backdoor attack, with certain activation functions being significantly more challenging to implement than others. Lastly, we discovered that our dynamic backdoor attack can be detected using an anomaly detection method based on the activation function's output. However, the detection method is only effective when the trigger feature is present, which presents a significant challenge for its practical application. To address this limitation, further research is required to develop more effective detection methods that can handle cases where the trigger feature is not present. This involves representing knowledge as a structured entity and leveraging it for type-based matching and logical inference to select relevant knowledge. This study employs an advanced algorithm to generate complete spectral models for a range of small oxygen-containing molecular cations.  By utilizing an active learning method to select and refine basis sets for these complex ions, we were able to create accurate theoretical descriptions of their electronic structures.  A key challenge in this area of research is the presence of weakly bound oxygen atoms within these molecules, making it difficult to distinguish true electrons from noise in numerical calculations.  To overcome this limitation, we developed an active thresholding technique to remove artificial electrons and focus on the real electrons more easily.  By combining this approach with active learning, we were able to create a more efficient and effective way to build complete spectral models for these complex ions.  As examples, we applied this method to create full spectral models for five small oxygen-containing molecular cations: water dimer cation, formic acid cation, acetic acid cation, carbonic acid cation, and hydrogen peroxide cation.  Using these models, we simulated infrared spectra for these molecules under different conditions and compared them with available experimental data.  The results show that our method produces accurate spectra in good agreement with experiments, with some errors due to the limitations of numerical calculations.  To further improve the accuracy of these models, we suggest using them in conjunction with experimental measurements and other theoretical methods, such as multi-configurational perturbation theory.  As computational power increases, we anticipate that this algorithm will become even more valuable for creating full spectral models for complex molecular systems.  In addition, we found that the active learning approach can also be applied to improve the basis set size for neutral molecules, such as water and formic acid, by identifying the most difficult to describe electrons and focusing on them first.  This led to a significant improvement in the convergence of total energies with increasing basis set size.  In summary, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of combining active learning with thresholding in creating full spectral models for complex molecular systems and highlights its broader potential for improving the description of difficult electronic systems. In pharmacology, accurate predictions from relational machine learning models are crucial for optimizing drug combinations and selecting relevant biological data. However, evaluating the performance of these models is complicated by the absence of standardized evaluation metrics and clear guidelines. Furthermore, the field's progress is hindered by a lack of publicly available data and models, hindering replication and comparison of results. To address these challenges, we present a framework consisting of novel evaluation metrics that prioritize both computational efficiency and substantive performance assessment. Additionally, we conduct experiments using multiple relational machine learning models and customize-designed datasets derived from real-world pharmacological data, encompassing topics such as cancer treatment, immunology, and virology. These experiments reveal that models exhibiting optimal performance according to our proposed evaluation criteria consistently outperform baseline models, indicating that our framework effectively identifies top-performing models. Notably, our findings suggest that specific relational machine learning models, namely TMAN and GIN, exhibit strong performance in predicting drug combinations and target relationships, respectively. Moreover, we observe that models leveraging graph attention mechanisms and hyperedge attention outperform their counterparts utilizing conventional attention mechanisms. Our work aims to advance the evaluation of relational machine learning models in pharmacology and facilitate comparable research replication. Distributed learning models often require multiple nodes to share their calculated model updates in a centralized location, which can be inefficient due to the high communication costs involved. This problem is particularly pronounced in scenarios where training data is fragmented across nodes with limited network connectivity. In such scenarios, the conventional distributed learning approach can be slow and impractical. This paper introduces a novel, node-centric, distributed learning framework inspired by random walk theory. In this new model, information flows locally between neighboring nodes, reducing the need for extensive communication with distant nodes. We examine the algorithm's convergence properties and provide guidelines for optimizing the number of iterations based on the nodes' geographical distribution. Theoretical performance guarantees are also established, taking into account the limited knowledge of nodes about their surroundings. Experimental results with both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness. In semi-supervised learning for medical image segmentation, generating high-quality results with minimal labels requires a strong model that generalizes well to unseen data. We propose an SS-UNet* model, which employs interpolation-based mixing as a regularization technique in semi-supervised learning. By combining two models - one trained on unlabeled data and the other on limited labeled data - we've observed consistent improvements in segmentation performance. Specifically, we utilized an advanced mixing strategy known as Frobenius norm based mixing, which outperformed traditional interpolation methods, resulting in a 5.34% ($p<0.01$) improvement in Dice scores without utilizing additional parameters. Furthermore, our approach outperformed leading semi-supervised segmentation methods while requiring significantly fewer labeled images (5 per class) to achieve comparable results. Abstract

Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has shown great potential in medical image segmentation by leveraging a large amount of unlabeled data along with a limited set of annotated images. However, achieving high accuracy with only a few labeled images remains a significant challenge. In this work, we propose an SSL framework called SS-UNet*, which employs an advanced mixing strategy known as Frobenius norm based mixing to combine two networks: one trained using unlabeled data and the other using a limited set of labeled data. We investigated the use of different norm types and found that the Frobenius norm yielded the best results, outperforming traditional interpolation methods without requiring additional parameters. Our experiments revealed a 5.34% ($p<0.01$) improvement in Dice scores and demonstrated that our approach outperformed leading semi-supervised segmentation methods using significantly fewer labeled images (5 per class) for multiple datasets. Furthermore, our results showed consistent improvements in segmentation performance with only 5% of the original dataset, indicating that our method effectively generalizes well to unseen data.

This study deviates from conventional approaches that separate scene analysis and synthesis. Instead, we propose a framework, Articulated Neural Rendering, which utilizes a single neural network to simultaneously analyze and reconstruct articulated scenes from multiple partial and distorted views of the scene. This approach builds upon the foundation of neural radiance fields by incorporating orientation and pose information, ultimately enabling dynamic object rendering. Our approach comprises a design that efficiently processes multiple views at once, which we show leads to a significant performance boost when compared to traditional approaches that process one view at a time. We also introduce a novel data augmentation technique specifically tailored for handling articulated scenes and pose variations, which we found to be a crucial component of our method's success. In multi-speech recognition systems, significant performance variations are observed across similar and dissimilar languages. This distinction suggests that knowledge transfer could enhance performance in languages with little similarity. We investigate this potential by applying transfer learning to a set of dissimilar languages within a single language family, specifically the Slavic languages, within the CzechSpeech dataset. We find that transfer learning yields a 5% absolute reduction in word error rates (WER) when combining just three Slavic languages (Czech, Polish, and Slovak) and a 14% WER reduction when incorporating the more dissimilar language of Slovenian. Notably, our baseline model achieves a 24% WER reduction on the Slovenian dataset without any data, achieving a WER of 48%. We also observe that the order of transfer learning matters, with starting from the most distant language resulting in worse performance. Additionally, we find that the distance between languages can be effectively gauged through the degree of orthographical standardization, with a straightforward metric showing a positive correlation with WER. We anticipate that our findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationships between languages in the context of multi-speech recognition systems. Furthermore, our results suggest that further research into transfer learning across languages with significant differences could lead to substantial improvements in future multi-speech recognition models. Discovering node embeddings for a graph before the structure is fully known is known as a challenging problem in modern graph learning. Novel algorithms that generate embeddings without needing the entire graph have shown promise, but it's difficult to assess their effectiveness because of the limited availability of real-world datasets tailored for this purpose. Our contribution is a groundbreaking dataset consisting of 139 episodes created from 6 real-world datasets, which serve as a benchmark for evaluating graph learning models. Each episode is a unique, partially revealed instance of a graph, allowing us to measure the accuracy of algorithms against actual graph learning tasks. Our experiments reveal that traditional algorithms are not sufficient for this type of node embedding, but excitingly, some novel algorithms exhibit high quality in predicting missing edges, community membership, and graph properties. Furthermore, we find that the performance of these algorithms is highly dependent on the degree of partial revelation in the graph. Ultimately, our findings provide valuable insights into the performance of graph learning models under partial revelation, which is crucial for developing more effective algorithms. The source code and datasets are openly accessible at https://parprogs.cs.pitt.edu/graph-eval-bar. The datasets will also be integrated into the PyTorch Geometric repository.

The connection between the mass of Primordial Black Holes (PBH) and the Cold Dark Matter (CDM) component of the universe is explored in this research. To establish this link, the team employed a technique to synchronize the formation of PBH and the onset of CDM cosmology. This method involved introducing a non-standard cosmological model in which the universe transitions from a dark matter-dominated state to the present day dark matter and baryonic matter co-domination, facilitated by the production of baryonic matter in the form of photons through Big Bang Nucleosynthesis. Utilizing this model, a range of 10^-17 to 10^-9 grams (or 10^4 to 10^7 GeV) for the mass of PBH, which constitutes nearly 100% of the CDM, is predicted based on a specific set of parameters. Additionally, the expected spectral form of the gravitational wave background generated by the collapse of these PBH is simulated using an N-body numerical code, and it is found that the resulting power spectrum, when normalized to the total CDM density within the mass range in question, yields a spectral shape that is consistent with the LISA sensitivity curve, making it potentially detectable with this instrument. Furthermore, a calculation of the total CDM density within this mass range, which is approximately 0.39 times the critical density of the universe, is also derived. This research also presents an analytical solution to the problem of identifying the mass spectrum of PBH formed through a given density perturbation spectrum, and it is demonstrated that the mass distribution of these PBH can be expressed in terms of the inverse of the cumulative distribution function of a standard normal distribution. We ran a series of high-resolution N-body simulations to investigate how a galaxy's central bar forms, specifically by examining the impact of its initial density distribution and velocity field on bar scale length and formation time. The models we analyzed included various bar-scale length configurations, set within a fixed galactic disk size, to better understand the bar formation process. Our simulations revealed that bar formation is accelerated in models featuring shorter initial scale lengths, with a nearly uniform relationship between the two. We also found that bar formation is influenced by a spiral density wave pattern, particularly when the wave pattern's natural frequency aligns with the bar's formation time. Based on our findings, we propose a new formula to estimate bar scale length, derived from a combination of factors including angular momentum distribution, velocity field, and spiral density wave patterns. Our research provides a theoretical framework for predicting bar scale length in a galaxy's disk, a key aspect of galaxy evolution. Furthermore, we found that bar formation can be slowed or even prevented by a massive, tightly packed central bar, and that the presence of a bar can influence the formation of spiral arms in a galaxy's outer regions. Our results also suggest that a galaxy's central bar can transform from a tightly packed, oval-shaped structure to a longer, bar-shaped form, potentially triggered by the migration of stars caused by a bar-induced spiral wave pattern. To address the issue of imbalanced data distribution in medical severity detection, we propose a novel 3D Contrastive Mixup Classification network, which incorporates a technique called contrastive learning to classify various types of medical pathologies. This method involves artificially generating artificial class mixups and modifying natural class samples to create artificial class samples, which are then used to create two datasets. Two 3D classification models are trained on these datasets to predict the class labels, and a loss function is calculated based on the predictions to help the network learn the differences between natural and artificial classes. Additionally, data augmentation techniques are employed to expand the dataset, which is used to generate a soft label for each data sample. The network's ability to produce these soft labels enables it to classify unseen medical data, which can be employed for improved baseline classification performance when data is scarce. Experimental evaluations utilizing the 3D Medical Segmentation Decathlon dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method, which outperforms existing methods in multiple challenges. For instance, our proposed method achieved a mean DSC score of 0.571 across all 21 ABIDE challenges, surpassing the previous best score of 0.546. Furthermore, our proposed method was evaluated on two additional publicly available datasets, namely the Pancreas-12 dataset and a custom-built dataset of cerebral small vessel disease, which were derived from T1-weighted MRI scans of 300 and 1000 subjects, respectively. These evaluations revealed a significant enhancement in classification accuracy, with mean DSC scores of 0.623 and 0.656, respectively, when utilizing a straightforward 3D UNet architecture. Notably, our proposed method outperformed conventional classification methods, including those employing ensemble techniques, by a substantial margin of 10-15%. Moreover, an intriguing finding from our experiments revealed a notable disparity in classification accuracy between two types of cerebral small vessel disease, which has significant implications for further research in this area. Consequently, our proposed 3D Contrastive Mixup Classification network offers a cutting-edge solution for the classification of various medical pathologies, which can be applied to a broad spectrum of medical imaging modalities and scenarios. Our proposed method aims to adapt Generalized Edit Distance (GED) to Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), allowing them to learn edit distances instead of relying on explicit computation. We initially assess this method's effectiveness in adapting pre-trained GNNs for multi-task graph classification tasks by comparing it to traditional transfer learning approaches. The results show that our proposed method outperforms baseline transfer learning techniques and achieves similar performance when using in-domain data. Furthermore, experiments with adapted data demonstrate that our approach matches the performance of models trained from scratch on new data, indicating that our GED-adapted model can effectively capture task knowledge. The success of our method is also analyzed through an ablation study and by examining the learned edit distances. Additionally, we observe that our approach enables the identification of distinct prototypes for each class, demonstrating its ability to generalize edit distances learned through adaptation to new, unseen instances. The code for our method is openly available at https://github.com/chen308/ged-gnn.

GdInO3 is a rare earth oxide with a Delafossit-style HfO3-type structure, where Gd+ ions form a triangular lattice while interacting via long-range forces. This study explores the magnetic properties of GdInO3 through both theoretical calculations and experimental analysis. Our calculations show that the Gd+ ions in GdInO3 possess an intrinsic spin-triplet chiral order, which is mediated by a multi-phonon process known as the Orstein process. This is confirmed by our experimental findings of magnetic scattering, specific heat, and NMR in GdInO3. These results provide a clear example of how magnetic interactions can be influenced by the lattice structure and phonon-mediated forces, ultimately giving rise to the unique spin-triplet chiral order observed in this material. This discovery opens up new avenues for research in rare earth oxides with similar lattice structures. Additionally, this study highlights the importance of combining theoretical and experimental approaches in understanding the complex magnetic interactions present in these materials. This is particularly relevant given the challenges associated with simulating such phenomena using computational methods alone. This study is also relevant to ongoing research in rare earth materials with unusual magnetic properties, which are being explored for their potential applications in spintronic devices. This paper explores two methods for fairly allocating indivisible goods among multiple agents. The first approach, round-robin ordering, assigns goods in a cyclical order based on agents' residual desires, ensuring each receives a fair share. The second method, cut-and-choose, involves randomly selecting a fair allocation. Our analysis shows the round-robin method guarantees at least as much fairness as the cut-and-choose method and provides an upper limit on the difference, measurable by calculating the ratio of the two methods' fairness indices. This ratio serves as a measure of how fairly the round-robin method is compared to the cut-and-choose method. It is also shown that this ratio has an upper limit of four, implying that even in the worst-case scenario, the round-robin method is at least half as fair as the cut-and-choose method. Furthermore, we discuss how to calculate the ratio of interest for any given instance and present computational results for various good types and agent preference structures. Additionally, we conducted an additional analysis where the round-robin method is compared to random allocation, finding that the worst-case ratio is 2.5, providing insight into the relative fairness of these allocation procedures. It is also demonstrated that both the cut-and-choose and round-robin methods ensure minimal residual desires among agents, guaranteeing a lower bound of at least half-fairness in their allocation processes. It is also shown that both methods always achieve full fairness when there are only two agents involved. It is also demonstrated that the round-robin method's allocation is at least half-fair in relation to the optimal allocation derived from the linear programming relaxation, providing a lower bound on its effectiveness. It is also found that the round-robin method's allocation is significantly closer to being full-fair in comparison to the cut-and-choose method when there are only two agents involved. It is also demonstrated that both the cut-and-choose and round-robin methods always result in residual desires among agents being at their minimum possible value, ensuring a level of fairness in their allocation processes. Pseudo-labeling is a prominent method for expanding target domain data through synthetic data, but its effectiveness depends heavily on high-quality pseudo labels. Obtaining accurate pseudo labels for diverse target images can be challenging due to labeling errors occurring more frequently in such cases. To address this issue, we propose an alternative approach called "Single-Image Averaging" (SIA) that leverages multiple translated versions of a single target image to produce a more accurate pseudo label. Specifically, SIA uses a self-enrichment strategy to average predictions from different translation tasks and pseudo labels, ultimately generating improved pseudo labels for each target image. Experimental results show that our proposed SIA method yields pseudo labels of higher quality than existing pseudo-labeling techniques and, when combined with synthetic data generated through SIA, leads to significant accuracy improvements in semantic segmentation tasks on various benchmark datasets. For instance, SIA achieves +4.4% absolute mIoU improvement on the Cityscapes validation set compared to the standard pseudo-labeling approach. Code and models are available at https://github.com/zhengyangfeng/SIA.

Our research reveals a significant number of HII regions located at greater galactocentric radii than typically found in spiral galaxies, specifically in the outer rings and in the spiral arms of UGC 8839. By comparing our findings to other spiral galaxies, such as M101 and M83, we observed a notable discrepancy in the distribution of HII regions within UGC 8839. Furthermore, our observations indicate smaller distances between HII regions in UGC 8839 when compared to M101 and M83. By constructing a distance-luminosity relation for these HII regions based on their intrinsic luminosity, we were able to determine that UGC 8839's HII regions are, on average, 1.5 magnitudes fainter than those in M101 and M83. This discrepancy in brightness suggests that UGC 8839's interstellar medium may be less gas-rich and less efficient at forming HII regions. Additionally, we observed a narrower range of metallicities within UGC 8839's HII region population when compared to M101 and 30 Doradus. We also identified a metallicity gradient of -0.02 dex/ kpc within the outer rings and a more pronounced gradient of -0.06 dex/ kpc within the spiral arms of UGC 8839. Our analysis of the line widths of these HII regions revealed a relatively low velocity dispersion, averaging around 10 km/s, which is consistent with a low mass and a young age for these regions. Researchers who work on dark matter often face a challenge in experimenting with very low-mass interactions. A novel approach called paleo-detectors offers a solution by connecting dark matter to its ancient cosmic history. By applying this approach, it's possible to enhance the understanding of dark matter-nucleon interactions in the low-mass range. We've developed a general framework for paleo-detectors that can be applied to various types of dark matter and different detection methods. To illustrate this, we've created specific simulations for scalar, vector, and axial-dark matter interactions using current and future dark matter detection technology. The results show that even with existing technology, paleo-detectors can significantly improve the detection of dark matter below a certain mass threshold. Furthermore, we've found that future detectors with upgraded sensitivity may significantly enhance the paleo-detector signal in this mass range, potentially revealing dark matter with a mass as low as 1-10 keV. To validate these findings, we've compared our simulations to theoretical predictions of dark matter properties based on indirect detection methods. In doing so, we've identified the range in which paleo-detectors can effectively operate in the mass range between 1 keV and the neutrino mass limit. Additionally, we've established that the optimal dark matter cutoff energy, which is a key parameter in the paleo-detector framework, is directly related to the detector's nuclear recoil energy and that it can be optimized to maximize the detection sensitivity. Finally, we've explored the implications of paleo-detectors on dark matter models that involve multiple components and interacting dark matter, highlighting the potential for these detectors to disentangle such models based on the dark matter velocity distribution function. Overall, the paleo-detector framework offers a promising approach to uncovering dark matter with low-mass interactions and has the potential to significantly contribute to the broader field of dark matter research. The rapid evolution of modern databases necessitates a thorough reevaluation of traditional data management systems, specifically regarding their data update histories. These histories hold valuable information, yet often go unmonitored and unsecured. A prominent approach to enhance security involves differential privacy, a method for restricting access to sensitive information while allowing the release of general, anonymized insights. However, the cost of private releases of data can be exorbitant, making it essential to prioritize the most critical updates. Prior studies have already identified essential updates in various settings but have overlooked the fundamental problem of identifying updates that merit privacy protection. In this work, we introduce an initial framework for this problem, formulating it as an optimization task where the primary updates to be privatized are chosen to minimize the overall cost of privacy, taking into account both data processing expenses and the risk of data breaches. We also develop a prototype database management system called DifferPrivDB, which can effectively implement this framework and provide secure data access in real-world scenarios. Experimental evaluations of DifferPrivDB demonstrate its capacity to handle substantial datasets efficiently and provide robust security against data breaches. Moreover, we observed a significant reduction in processing costs when prioritizing critical updates, leading to even better performance improvements. DifferPrivDB is available for download at https://differprivdb.cs.umn.edu/. For further information, please refer to the accompanying technical report. Understanding how the performance of machine learning models improves with additional features from a pre-specified set is crucial for many applications, particularly those involving feature selection. We introduce a novel framework that leverages the Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores (MUCs) from the theory of Boolean Satisfiability to create a family of efficient algorithms for ranking feature importance. These algorithms can handle large-scale datasets by only requiring a small portion of computational power compared to existing methods during the feature selection process. Furthermore, once the initial features have been identified, the models can be refined with just a few hundred to a few thousand evaluations, significantly reducing the time and resources needed. This enables the exploration of a wide range of scenarios that reflect real-world scenarios more accurately. In our experiments, our approach demonstrates superior performance and faster convergence when compared to the state-of-the-art method, Linear Correlation-based Feature Importance, both on artificial and real-world datasets. Notably, our results on real-world datasets show a 2-5 orders of magnitude improvement in computational efficiency. Additionally, our findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between necessary and sufficient conditions for predicting model performance and emphasize the value of incorporating counterfactual evidence when assessing feature importance. The code for our algorithms is openly available at https://github.com/alexmurray/FeatureImportance.

The accurate recognition and segmentation of surgical instruments are critical for developing effective automation in operating rooms. To address this challenge, we introduce the Dual Decoder Attention Network (DDANet), a novel attention-based model that simultaneously identifies and outlines the code names of surgical tools on multiple organs on the abdominal wall during a laparoscopic procedure. Compared to other advanced deep learning techniques, our model showcases superior performance in both tasks according to our experimental data. Specifically, our findings reveal a significant improvement of 11.4% in code name recognition and a 15.6% enhancement in average code name accuracy when considering context from the abdominal wall. Our attention mechanism-driven design also yields a notable 14.5% increase in R-50-based instrument segmentation accuracy when assessed with the COCO metric. Moreover, our model's ability to generalize across various code names and organs is further highlighted by our results. To facilitate further research, we introduce LS-SmartWash, a multi-code name, multi-organ dataset that includes 24 distinct code names and incorporates data from two distinct datasets. This dataset comprises 1,500 annotated data samples following a standardized format that is both easy to understand and utilize. It is available for download at https://github.com/ChenChen9527/LS-SmartWash. The code for our model can also be accessed at https://github.com/ChenChen9527/DDANet. As the first dataset of its kind to incorporate multiple code names and organs, LS-SmartWash offers researchers a unique platform to explore attention-based models in the context of surgical instrument recognition and segmentation. Deep learning techniques for person re-identification (ReID) have significantly advanced in recent years. Nevertheless, the limited data and labeling costs hinder the development and practical applications of ReID. To address this challenge, unsupervised ReID methods have been proposed and achieved notable progress. These methods aim to learn from unlabeled data with reordering or distillation techniques, often incorporating contrastive learning to handle the disorderd identity information. Our research reveals that contrastive learning's primary function is to enhance the robustness of feature extractors against variations in lighting, pose, and background, while neglecting the inherent structure of identities. To tackle this issue, we introduce a new framework called Unsupervised Hierarchical Contrastive Learning (UHCL) that extracts identities' hierarchical structural information for alleviating the encoding of superficial variations into distinct identities. Specifically, UHCL incorporates a hierarchical contrastive learning module to organize identities in a prototypical tree structure, enabling the efficient retrieval of identities within a single prototype. Experimental evaluations on multiple public datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over the existing state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at: https://github.com/zhengzheng-zhang/UHCL.

This paper presents a new value-at-risk (VaR) forecasting model based on the Extreme Studentized Process (ESP), an advancement over traditional GARCH models. To ensure model stability and efficiency, we employ the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) for estimation. We then conduct a simulation study and a real-world application to evaluate the performance of the new model, followed by a comparison of its forecasting accuracy to that of the GARCH model using backtesting methods. All results indicate that the proposed VaR forecasting model outperforms the GARCH model. Furthermore, we discuss the potential applications and advantages of utilizing the ESP for VaR forecasting. However, it is essential to acknowledge that the package is no longer actively maintained by the original creators. Nonetheless, the package remains a valuable resource for researchers seeking to apply the Conditional ESP model. Futhermore, the paper includes an overview of related work in the field of VaR forecasting, encompassing both traditional and modern approaches utilizing machine learning techniques. Ultimately, the paper contributes meaningfully to the field of VaR forecasting through the innovative introduction of the Conditional ESP model. Our research examines the relationships between quark mass, the pion's distribution amplitude, and the pion's form factor $f_K$, utilizing lattice QCD techniques and varying the quark masses in a manner reflective of how quark masses are typically expressed - in units of the average light quark mass $\hat m$ or individual masses $m_u$, $m_d$, and $m_s$. We calculate the pion's ground-state characteristics at multiple $\hat m$ values, finding the dependence on individual quark masses $m_u$, $m_d$, and $m_s$ to be nearly imperceptible. Consequently, the distinction between using $\hat m$ or individual quark masses becomes negligible for our results, indicating that the choice of quark mass parametrization has a minimal impact of approximately $1\%$ when considering the chiral regime. Notably, the ratio $f_K/f_\pi$ exhibits little variation with changes in quark mass, displaying a degree of invariance that is consistent with our findings of the quark mass's minimal impact on the pion itself. Furthermore, our lattice data are in line with the predictions made by chiral perturbation theory. Additionally, we derive the $SU(2)$ Nambu-Goldstone boson low-energy effective theory at order $p^2$ and include the $K$-meson's form factor $f_K$, yielding a fit to our lattice data and extracting the low-energy constants $B_0$, $B_1$, $B_2$, and $L_1$, which are in line with theoretical predictions and previous lattice studies. Consequently, we calculate the $K$-meson's form factor $f_K$ at a pion momentum of $300\text{ MeV}$ to be $1.44\pm 0.01$, demonstrating a level of precision that is currently attainable with lattice QCD. Moreover, our research provides a detailed derivation of the pion's distribution amplitude, expressed in terms of Gegenbauer polynomials, and enables a comparison with the conventional Bochler et al. parameterization, revealing a level of variation of approximately $1\%$. Classical T Tauri stars (CTTSs) are notable for their strong magnetic fields and unpredictable matter circulation patterns, which enable the transport of angular momentum and facilitate disk evolution. However, the CTTSs' accretion process is remarkably inconsistent, with variations often exceeding three orders of magnitude, which poses a challenge for existing models. The issue lies in explaining the relatively stable widths of the Balmer and other spectral lines in these stars, which suggests a stable, friction-dominated regime exists, capable of withstanding extreme changes in accretion rates. The proposed model for this equilibrium, which involves a thin, friction-dominated disk altimeter, is examined in the context of existing observations and is shown to be viable. The model is applied to a sample of 44 objects from the LUMIERE survey, which includes a group of weak-line T Tauri stars, in order to determine the relationship between the line width and the level of mass accretion. The results indicate a linear relationship between line width and mass accretion rate, which can be expressed as $\Delta v \propto \dot{M}^{0.97\pm0.19}$. The model is further validated by comparing its predictions for the line width at a given mass accretion rate to those generated by other models, which involve global disk simulations. The comparison shows that the proposed model accurately predicts the line width for mass accretion rates above $10^{-7} \dot{M}_{\mathrm{Edd}}$, while the other models are limited to rates below $10^{-6} \dot{M}_{\mathrm{Edd}}$.
